questions.stem: A 24-year-old woman begins taking a combined oral contraceptive pill. Two months later, mid-cycle ultrasonography shows no dominant ovarian follicle, and serum studies show no mid-cycle luteinizing hormone surge. Which of the following actions of the estrogen component best explains these findings?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Direct blockade of ovarian receptors for follicle-stimulating hormone

choices.label: B
choices.text: Increased pulsatile release of gonadotropin-releasing hormone

choices.label: C
choices.text: Negative feedback suppression of follicle-stimulating hormone release

choices.label: D
choices.text: Thickening of cervical mucus to block sperm penetration

choices.label: E
choices.text: Thinning of the endometrium to prevent implantation

explanation.summary: Estrogen in combined OCPs prevents ovulation by suppressing FSH, which blocks follicular development and therefore the LH surge.
explanation.whyCorrect: The most important mechanism of the estrogen component is negative feedback suppression of FSH, preventing the follicle development that normally follows the FSH rise around day 3-4 of the cycle. With no growing follicle, there is no ovulatory LH surge on day 12-13, and even an LH surge would have no effect without a mature follicle.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Estrogen works by feedback suppression of gonadotropin release, not by blocking ovarian gonadotropin receptors; the LH surge is absent because no follicle develops.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Hormonal contraception suppresses, rather than increases, gonadotropin drive; increased GnRH pulsatility would promote, not prevent, follicle growth.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Cervical mucus thickening is an action of the progestin component, and it would not abolish follicle growth or the LH surge.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Endometrial thinning is a progestin effect that prevents implantation; it does not explain absent follicular development.

questions.stem: A 37-year-old woman who smokes one pack of cigarettes daily requests contraception. She has no other medical problems, and her blood pressure is normal. She says she often forgets daily medications. Which of the following is the most appropriate contraceptive method for this patient?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Combined estrogen-progestin oral contraceptive pills

choices.label: B
choices.text: Combined estrogen-progestin transdermal patch

choices.label: C
choices.text: Combined estrogen-progestin vaginal ring

choices.label: D
choices.text: Extended-cycle combined oral contraceptive pills

choices.label: E
choices.text: Progestin-containing subdermal implant

explanation.summary: Smokers older than 35 should not receive estrogen-containing contraception; a progestin-only long-acting method fits both her risk profile and her adherence needs.
explanation.whyCorrect: Estrogen increases coagulability, and smokers older than 35 years are at increased risk of clots, so combined methods should not be prescribed for them. The progestin subdermal implant avoids estrogen entirely, requires no daily action for 5 years, and has a pregnancy rate of 0.05%.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Combined pills contain estrogen, which should not be prescribed to smokers older than 35 because of clotting risk, and daily pills poorly suit a forgetful patient.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The patch delivers combined estrogen-progestin, carrying the same estrogen clotting concern in a smoker older than 35.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The vaginal ring is also a combined estrogen-progestin method and is inappropriate for this smoker over 35.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Extended-cycle pills change the placebo schedule but still contain estrogen and still demand daily adherence.

questions.stem: A 29-year-old woman requests combined oral contraceptive pills. Which of the following findings in her history is an absolute contraindication to prescribing them?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Gallbladder disease with prior biliary colic

choices.label: B
choices.text: Hypertension that is well controlled on medication

choices.label: C
choices.text: Maternal age older than 45 years at her own birth

choices.label: D
choices.text: Migraine headaches preceded by a visual aura

choices.label: E
choices.text: Smoking five cigarettes daily at her current age

explanation.summary: Migraine with aura is an absolute contraindication to combined oral contraceptives.
explanation.whyCorrect: Absolute contraindications to combined OCPs include migraine with aura, along with pregnancy, thromboembolic disorders, coronary artery disease or stroke, uncontrolled hypertension, breast cancer or other hormone-dependent neoplasms, and liver tumors.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Gallbladder disease is a relative, not absolute, contraindication; estrogen and progesterone increase the risk of gallstones.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Uncontrolled hypertension is the absolute contraindication; hypertension in general is listed as relative.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The relative contraindication concerns the patient herself being older than 45 years, not her mother's age.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Smoking is a relative contraindication, reflecting increased clotting risk after age 35; she is 29.

questions.stem: A 38-year-old woman is found to have a hepatocellular adenoma on abdominal imaging performed for another reason. Which of the following elements of her history most likely contributed to development of this lesion?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A single dose of levonorgestrel emergency contraception

choices.label: B
choices.text: Depot medroxyprogesterone injections for 2 years

choices.label: C
choices.text: Use of a copper intrauterine device for 8 years

choices.label: D
choices.text: Use of a progestin-only minipill for 1 year

choices.label: E
choices.text: Use of estrogen-containing oral contraceptives for 8 years

explanation.summary: Long-term use of estrogen-containing OCPs increases the risk of hepatocellular adenoma.
explanation.whyCorrect: The risk of hepatocellular adenoma (benign liver tumor) is increased in women using estrogen-containing oral contraceptives, and the risk rises with long-term use of more than 5 years. About 4% of these tumors become malignant.

whyWrongByChoice.A: A single dose of a progestin emergency contraceptive is not the described long-term estrogen exposure that drives adenoma risk.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The adenoma risk is tied to estrogen-containing contraceptives; medroxyprogesterone is a progestin-only injection.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The copper IUD is nonhormonal, acting locally through sperm-toxic copper ions, and is not linked to hepatic adenomas.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The minipill contains progestin only; the lesion is associated with estrogen-containing pills used long term.

questions.stem: A 27-year-old woman is 3 months postpartum and exclusively breastfeeding; lactation is well established. She requests an oral contraceptive, and a progestin-only pill is recommended rather than a combined pill. Which of the following is the best rationale for this recommendation?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Combined pills lose contraceptive efficacy in lactating patients

choices.label: B
choices.text: Estrogen can interfere with milk supply and increase postpartum thrombosis risk

choices.label: C
choices.text: Estrogen in breast milk causes virilization of the nursing infant

choices.label: D
choices.text: Progestin-only pills additionally protect against sexually transmitted infections

choices.label: E
choices.text: Progestins stimulate prolactin secretion and thereby augment milk production

explanation.summary: Progestin-only methods are preferred during breastfeeding because estrogen can reduce milk supply and raise postpartum thrombosis risk.
explanation.whyCorrect: Combined methods are avoided in breastfeeding women because estrogen can interfere with milk supply and increase the risk of postpartum thrombosis. Because progesterone blocks prolactin's stimulation of milk synthesis, even progestin-only hormonal contraception should begin only after lactation is well established, as it is here.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The concern with combined pills in lactation is milk supply and clot risk, not a loss of contraceptive efficacy.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Infant virilization from estrogen in breast milk is not the described concern; the issues are maternal milk supply and thrombosis.
whyWrongByChoice.D: No hormonal pill protects against sexually transmitted infections; condoms provide STI protection.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Progesterone blocks, rather than stimulates, the effect of prolactin on milk synthesis, which is why hormonal methods wait until lactation is established.

questions.stem: A 25-year-old woman uses a traditional progestin-only minipill. During the middle of her cycle, she takes her pill 5 hours later than her usual time and has intercourse that evening. Her increased risk of contraceptive failure is best explained by loss of which of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Local copper-mediated toxicity to sperm within the uterus

choices.label: B
choices.text: Prolactin-mediated suppression of gonadotropin-releasing hormone

choices.label: C
choices.text: Reliable ovulation suppression, the pill's primary mechanism of action

choices.label: D
choices.text: Suppression of FSH by the pill's estrogen component

choices.label: E
choices.text: Thickened cervical mucus, the pill's primary mechanism of action

explanation.summary: The traditional minipill works mainly by thickening cervical mucus, so even a 4-6 hour dosing delay mid-cycle can cause contraceptive failure.
explanation.whyCorrect: Because the traditional minipill's primary mechanism is thickening cervical mucus rather than preventing ovulation, strict adherence to dosing time is critical. Taking the pill even 4-6 hours late in the middle of a cycle can allow the mucus barrier to lapse and result in contraceptive failure.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Copper-mediated sperm toxicity is the mechanism of the copper IUD, not of any pill.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Prolactin-mediated GnRH suppression is the mechanism of lactational amenorrhea, not of the minipill.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The traditional minipill does not reliably stop ovulation; among progestin-only options, the implant, injection, and Slynd do.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The minipill contains no estrogen, so FSH suppression by estrogen is not part of its action.

questions.stem: A 26-year-old woman becomes pregnant while prescribed combined oral contraceptive pills. Her physician notes that although this method is more than 99% effective in theory, its actual efficacy is closer to 91%. Which of the following most likely explains this difference?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Development of tolerance to the hormones over time

choices.label: B
choices.text: Inherited resistance to progestin at its receptor

choices.label: C
choices.text: Neutralization of the hormones by vaginal secretions

choices.label: D
choices.text: Pills that were missed or taken at the wrong time

choices.label: E
choices.text: Variability in hormone content between pill batches

explanation.summary: The gap between theoretical (>99%) and actual (~91%) OCP efficacy comes from user error, chiefly missed or mistimed pills.
explanation.whyCorrect: Theoretical efficacy describes perfect use, while actual efficacy reflects typical use with user error. For oral contraceptives the gap arises because patients forget one or more pills in a package or take pills at the wrong time; methods requiring no user action, like the IUD and implant, have nearly identical theoretical and actual efficacy.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Hormone tolerance is not a described phenomenon with OCPs; adherence failures explain typical-use pregnancies.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Receptor-level progestin resistance is not the explanation given for real-world failures.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Oral pills act systemically after ingestion; vaginal secretions do not neutralize them.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Manufacturing variability is not the described cause; the efficacy gap is attributed to how patients use the method.

questions.stem: A 21-year-old college student with a busy schedule requests contraception. She wants a reversible method, doubts she could remember a daily pill, and asks for the option with the lowest pregnancy rate. Which of the following methods best meets her request?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Combined estrogen-progestin patch

choices.label: B
choices.text: Combined oral contraceptive pills

choices.label: C
choices.text: Diaphragm used with spermicide

choices.label: D
choices.text: Male condom with each act of intercourse

choices.label: E
choices.text: Progesterone subdermal implant

explanation.summary: The subdermal implant is the most effective reversible method, with a 0.05% pregnancy rate and no daily user action.
explanation.whyCorrect: The progesterone subdermal implant has the lowest pregnancy rate of any method (0.05%), is reversible, and lasts up to 5 years. Because a provider places it and no patient action is required, its theoretical and actual efficacy are nearly identical, unlike user-dependent methods.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The patch also carries a 9% pregnancy rate and requires weekly changes, far less effective than the implant.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Oral pills have a 9% typical-use pregnancy rate and require exactly the daily adherence she doubts she can maintain.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The diaphragm has a 12% pregnancy rate, must be used with spermicide, and depends on correct use each time.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Condoms have an 18% pregnancy rate; they add STI protection but are not the most effective method.

questions.stem: A 27-year-old woman requests long-acting contraception but wants to avoid all hormonal methods. A copper-containing intrauterine device is placed. Which of the following best describes the mechanism by which this device prevents pregnancy?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Copper ions create a local inflammatory, sperm-toxic environment that impairs sperm motility

choices.label: B
choices.text: Copper ions directly suppress ovarian follicular development and ovulation each cycle

choices.label: C
choices.text: Locally released progestin thickens cervical mucus at the internal cervical os

choices.label: D
choices.text: Systemic absorption of copper suppresses the mid-cycle LH surge from the anterior pituitary gland

choices.label: E
choices.text: The device mechanically seals the cervical canal so that sperm cannot enter the uterus

explanation.summary: The copper IUD prevents fertilization through a local inflammatory, sperm-toxic uterine environment without suppressing ovulation.
explanation.whyCorrect: Copper ions create a local inflammatory, sperm-toxic uterine environment that impairs sperm motility and transport, preventing fertilization. It is the only nonhormonal contraceptive device, works without suppressing ovulation, and lasts 10 years.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Ovulation is not suppressed by the copper IUD; follicular development continues normally.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The copper IUD releases no hormone; cervical mucus thickening is the action of progestin-containing methods.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The device acts locally within the uterus; it does not work by systemic suppression of the LH surge.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Sealing the cervix describes barrier devices like the cervical cap or diaphragm, not the IUD.

questions.stem: A 22-year-old woman had unprotected intercourse 4 days ago and has not yet ovulated this cycle. She requests emergency contraception. Which of the following is the most appropriate option at this time?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Beginning a fertility awareness-based method

choices.label: B
choices.text: Depot medroxyprogesterone intramuscular injection

choices.label: C
choices.text: Levonorgestrel emergency contraceptive pill

choices.label: D
choices.text: Starting a daily combined oral contraceptive pack

choices.label: E
choices.text: Ulipristal acetate emergency contraceptive pill

explanation.summary: Ulipristal acetate can be used up to 5 days after unprotected intercourse, whereas levonorgestrel is limited to 3 days.
explanation.whyCorrect: Emergency contraception prevents or delays ovulation when used before ovulation, and it can work for up to 5 days after unprotected intercourse. At 4 days, ulipristal acetate (Ella), which is effective up to 5 days but requires a prescription, is the appropriate choice.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Fertility awareness prevents future exposures by identifying fertile days; it cannot reduce risk from intercourse 4 days ago.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The medroxyprogesterone injection is a routine every-12-weeks contraceptive, not an emergency method for intercourse that already occurred.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Levonorgestrel (Plan B) can be used up to 3 days after unprotected sex, and its efficacy falls steeply with time; the window has passed at 4 days.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Daily combined pills are routine contraception going forward; they are not a method of emergency contraception after intercourse.

questions.stem: A 24-year-old woman is 2 months postpartum, breastfeeds exclusively at least every 4 hours, and has had no return of menses. She has not used any contraceptive method yet has not become pregnant despite regular intercourse. Which of the following best explains her current protection from pregnancy?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Elevated postpartum estrogen suppresses follicle-stimulating hormone

choices.label: B
choices.text: High postpartum progesterone keeps cervical mucus impenetrable to sperm

choices.label: C
choices.text: Persistent uterine inflammation after delivery prevents implantation

choices.label: D
choices.text: Prolactin acts directly on the ovary to destroy developing follicles

choices.label: E
choices.text: Prolactin and the suckling stimulus suppress gonadotropin-releasing hormone release

explanation.summary: Lactational amenorrhea works because prolactin and the suckling stimulus both suppress GnRH release, preventing ovulation.
explanation.whyCorrect: Breastfeeding can be an effective contraceptive within the first 6 months after delivery when nursing is exclusive and occurs at least every 4 hours. Both the prolactin stimulated by suckling and the suckling stimulus itself suppress GnRH release, which prevents ovulation; once menses return, another method is needed.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The effect is driven by prolactin and suckling suppressing GnRH, not by elevated estrogen suppressing FSH.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The lactational mechanism is prevention of ovulation via GnRH suppression, not a cervical mucus barrier.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Postpartum uterine inflammation blocking implantation is not the described mechanism of lactational contraception.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Prolactin's contraceptive effect is central suppression of GnRH, not direct destruction of ovarian follicles.

questions.stem: A 30-year-old woman has taken combined oral contraceptive pills for 9 years. During counseling, her physician notes that long-term use of these pills is associated with a reduced risk of ovarian cancer. Which of the following mechanisms most likely underlies this protective effect?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A decreased number of ovulatory cycles over time

choices.label: B
choices.text: Chronic thickening of the cervical mucus barrier

choices.label: C
choices.text: Progressive thinning of the endometrial lining

choices.label: D
choices.text: Reduced proliferation of hormone-responsive breast tissue

choices.label: E
choices.text: Suppression of hepatic adenoma formation

explanation.summary: Long-term combined OCP use lowers ovarian cancer risk, probably because of decreased ovulation.
explanation.whyCorrect: Long-term use of combined oral contraceptives is associated with a reduced risk of ovarian cancer, probably due to decreased ovulation, since the pills suppress follicular development and the ovulatory LH surge cycle after cycle.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Cervical mucus thickening is a contraceptive mechanism; it has no bearing on ovarian cancer risk.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Endometrial thinning is the mechanism proposed for the lower rate of endometrial cancer, a different protective effect.
whyWrongByChoice.D: OCPs can increase proliferation of hormone-responsive tissue and may accelerate growth of existing breast cancers; this is not an ovarian protective mechanism.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Estrogen-containing pills increase, not suppress, hepatocellular adenoma risk, and that has no protective link to the ovary.

questions.stem: A physician uses the WHO Medical Eligibility Criteria for Contraceptive Use to evaluate methods for a patient with a chronic medical condition. One method is classified as Category 4 for her condition. Which of the following is the correct interpretation of this classification?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The method is effective for this patient only with perfect use

choices.label: B
choices.text: The method may be used by this patient without any restrictions

choices.label: C
choices.text: The method must be placed by a provider rather than the patient

choices.label: D
choices.text: The method poses an unacceptable health risk for this patient

choices.label: E
choices.text: The method protects this patient against sexually transmitted infections

explanation.summary: In the WHO Medical Eligibility Criteria, Category 4 means a contraceptive method is an unacceptable health risk for a patient with that condition.
explanation.whyCorrect: The WHO Medical Eligibility Criteria for Contraceptive Use provides evidence-based guidance on the safety of contraceptive methods for women with specific characteristics or medical conditions. It categorizes methods from Category 1, meaning no restrictions for use, to Category 4, meaning the method carries an unacceptable health risk for that patient.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The categories address safety of a method for a given condition, not the difference between perfect and typical use.
whyWrongByChoice.B: No restrictions for use describes Category 1, the opposite end of the eligibility scale.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Provider placement is a feature of devices like IUDs and implants; it is not what the eligibility categories describe.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The criteria classify health risk; they say nothing about STI protection, which among methods is provided by condoms.

questions.stem: A 42-year-old man elects to undergo surgical sterilization. During the procedure, a paired structure is ligated bilaterally through small scrotal incisions. Ligation of which of the following structures accomplishes contraception in this patient?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Ductus deferens

choices.label: B
choices.text: Epididymis

choices.label: C
choices.text: Prostatic urethra

choices.label: D
choices.text: Seminal vesicle

choices.label: E
choices.text: Seminiferous tubule

explanation.summary: Vasectomy is ligation of the paired ductus deferens, which prevents sperm transport from the testes to the urethra.
explanation.whyCorrect: Vasectomy involves ligation of the paired ductus deferens (also called vas deferens). This blocks the transport of sperm from the testes to the urethra, preventing sperm from being ejaculated.

whyWrongByChoice.B: The epididymis is not the structure ligated in vasectomy; the procedure interrupts the ductus deferens.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The urethra is the destination sperm can no longer reach after vasectomy; it is not itself ligated.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The seminal vesicles are not ligated in vasectomy; contraception comes from blocking the sperm-conducting duct.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Seminiferous tubules within the testis are the site of sperm production and are not ligated in this procedure.

questions.stem: A 42-year-old woman underwent tubal ligation at age 35 years. She has remarried and requests surgical reversal so she can attempt pregnancy. Which of the following is the most accurate counseling regarding her chance of pregnancy after reversal?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A pregnancy rate of about 30% to 40%

choices.label: B
choices.text: A pregnancy rate of about 75% to 80%

choices.label: C
choices.text: A pregnancy rate of greater than 99%

choices.label: D
choices.text: A pregnancy rate of less than 1%

choices.label: E
choices.text: Fertility cannot be restored after tubal ligation

explanation.summary: After reversal of tubal ligation, the pregnancy rate in women older than 40 years falls to 30% to 40%.
explanation.whyCorrect: Surgical sterilization can be reversed with varying success. After reversal of tubal ligation, the pregnancy rate in women younger than 35 years is 75% to 80%, but in women older than 40 years it decreases to 30% to 40%. This patient is 42, so the lower range applies.

whyWrongByChoice.B: 75% to 80% is the post-reversal pregnancy rate for women younger than 35 years, not for a 42-year-old.
whyWrongByChoice.C: No figure approaching certainty is described for reversal; even the younger group reaches only 75% to 80%.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Less than 1% understates her chances; reversal in her age group still yields pregnancy in roughly a third of women.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Sterilization procedures can be reversed with varying success, so counseling that fertility can never return is inaccurate.

questions.stem: A large prospective cohort study enrolled more than 9,000 women, provided tiered contraceptive counseling that presented methods in order of effectiveness, and offered any reversible method at no cost for 2 to 3 years. Compared with national utilization patterns at the time, most participants chose which of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Combined oral contraceptive pills taken daily

choices.label: B
choices.text: Fertility awareness-based (rhythm) methods

choices.label: C
choices.text: Intrauterine devices and subdermal implants

choices.label: D
choices.text: Male condoms and other barrier methods

choices.label: E
choices.text: Transdermal contraceptive patches and vaginal rings

explanation.summary: When cost, education, and access barriers were removed in the Contraceptive CHOICE Project, 75% of participants chose long-acting reversible contraception.
explanation.whyCorrect: The Contraceptive CHOICE Project removed the barriers of cost, education gaps, and access, and 75% of participants chose LARC methods: 46% the levonorgestrel IUD, 12% the copper IUD, and 17% the subdermal implant. This was dramatically higher than the roughly 11% national LARC utilization rate at the time, and teenage pregnancy among participants was far lower than national rates (3.4% vs 15.8%).

whyWrongByChoice.A: Oral pills were not the dominant choice; three-quarters of participants selected long-acting reversible methods instead.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Fertility awareness-based methods were not the leading choice when highly effective methods were freely available.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Condoms are barrier methods at the low-effectiveness end of tiered counseling and were not what most participants chose.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Patches and rings are shorter-acting combined methods and did not account for the majority of choices.

questions.stem: A 26-year-old woman using a fertility awareness-based method observes that in the first half of her menstrual cycle, before ovulation, her cervical mucus becomes thin and easily penetrable by sperm. Which of the following hormonal effects best explains this observation?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Estrogen thickens the cervical mucus during the follicular phase

choices.label: B
choices.text: Estrogen thins the cervical mucus during the follicular phase

choices.label: C
choices.text: Luteinizing hormone thickens the cervical mucus at mid-cycle

choices.label: D
choices.text: Progesterone thins the cervical mucus during the follicular phase

choices.label: E
choices.text: Progesterone thins the cervical mucus during the luteal phase

explanation.summary: In the natural cycle, follicular-phase estrogen thins cervical mucus to facilitate sperm entry, while luteal-phase progesterone thickens it.
explanation.whyCorrect: Cervical mucus changes across the menstrual cycle. In the follicular phase, before ovulation, estrogen thins the mucus to facilitate entry of sperm and increase the potential for fertilization. The opposite occurs in the luteal phase, when progesterone thickens the mucus into a barrier that blocks sperm.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Estrogen thins rather than thickens mucus in the follicular phase; thickening is the progesterone effect after ovulation.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The described mucus changes are attributed to estrogen and progesterone, not to luteinizing hormone.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Progesterone dominates the luteal phase and thickens mucus; the follicular-phase thinning is driven by estrogen.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Progesterone acts in the luteal phase, but its effect is to thicken mucus into a sperm barrier, not to thin it.

questions.stem: A 23-year-old woman takes a monophasic combined oral contraceptive from a 28-pill pack containing 21 active pills followed by 7 placebo pills. She asks why she bleeds during the last week of each pack. Which of the following best explains this bleeding?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A fertilized egg fails to implant at the end of each pill pack

choices.label: B
choices.text: Estrogen accumulates during the placebo week and causes bleeding

choices.label: C
choices.text: Ovulation occurs during the placebo week and triggers menstruation

choices.label: D
choices.text: The drop in hormone levels stimulates shedding of the uterine lining

choices.label: E
choices.text: The placebo pills contain a drug that induces endometrial shedding

explanation.summary: Bleeding during the placebo week is a withdrawal bleed caused by the drop in hormone levels, which stimulates shedding of the uterine lining.
explanation.whyCorrect: Monophasic packs typically contain 21 active pills and 4 to 7 placebos. Women usually menstruate during the placebo week because the drop in hormone levels stimulates shedding of the uterine lining, called a withdrawal bleed. The placebos themselves exist only to support adherence by preserving the daily pill routine.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The bleed reflects hormone withdrawal, not a failed implantation event each month.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Hormone levels fall, rather than accumulate, during the placebo week; that withdrawal is what triggers bleeding.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The combined pill suppresses follicular development and the LH surge, so ovulation is not occurring during the placebo week.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Placebo pills contain no hormone or active drug; their purpose is to maintain the daily habit of pill-taking.

questions.stem: A physician prescribes a multiphasic combined oral contraceptive designed to reduce hormonal adverse effects by mimicking the natural menstrual cycle. The chosen formulation is biphasic. Which of the following describes the hormone dosing of this pill?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A fixed estrogen dose with the progestin increased in the second half of the month

choices.label: B
choices.text: A progestin-only formulation with the dose doubled at mid-cycle

choices.label: C
choices.text: Active pills taken continuously with no placebo week in any month

choices.label: D
choices.text: An increase in the dose of estrogen, progestin, or both every week of the month

choices.label: E
choices.text: The same dose of estrogen and progestin in every active pill in the pack

explanation.summary: Biphasic pills keep the estrogen dose fixed and increase the progestin in the second half of the month.
explanation.whyCorrect: Multiphasic pills were developed to reduce the adverse effects of OCP hormones by mimicking the natural cycle, increasing hormone amounts as the month proceeds. Biphasic pills contain a fixed dose of estrogen with the progestin increased in the second half of the month.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Biphasic pills are combined estrogen-progestin formulations, not progestin-only products.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Continuous dosing with no placebo week describes continuous OCPs, which is a schedule pattern rather than biphasic dosing.
whyWrongByChoice.D: A weekly increase in estrogen, progestin, or both describes triphasic pills, not biphasic ones.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Identical dosing in every active pill describes a monophasic formulation.

questions.stem: A 27-year-old woman taking a standard 28-day combined oral contraceptive wants fewer menstrual periods each year but would like to keep a scheduled withdrawal bleed a few times per year. Which of the following formulations best meets her preference?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Continuous combined oral contraceptive pills

choices.label: B
choices.text: Extended-cycle combined oral contraceptive pills

choices.label: C
choices.text: Monophasic pills in a standard 28-day pack

choices.label: D
choices.text: Traditional progestin-only contraceptive pills

choices.label: E
choices.text: Triphasic pills in a standard 28-day pack

explanation.summary: Extended-cycle OCPs place the placebo week at the end of several months, producing fewer menstrual cycles per year while retaining periodic withdrawal bleeds.
explanation.whyCorrect: Extended-cycle OCPs have a placebo week at the end of several months instead of after every 3 weeks, which results in fewer menstrual cycles per year. Because a placebo week still occurs periodically, she keeps a scheduled withdrawal bleed a few times per year, exactly as she prefers.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Continuous OCPs have no placebo week at all, so they do not provide the periodic scheduled bleed she wants to keep.
whyWrongByChoice.C: A standard 28-day monophasic pack produces a withdrawal bleed every month, which is what she is trying to reduce.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The progestin-only pill is chosen for estrogen avoidance and does not provide the extended-schedule bleed pattern she requests.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Triphasic dosing changes hormone amounts each week to reduce adverse effects; in a 28-day pack it still yields monthly bleeds.

questions.stem: A 33-year-old woman has taken combined oral contraceptive pills for 8 years. Her physician tells her that long-term use is associated with a lower rate of endometrial cancer. Which of the following most likely explains this protective effect?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A decreased number of ovulatory cycles over years of use

choices.label: B
choices.text: Lower androgen synthesis from decreased luteinizing hormone

choices.label: C
choices.text: Reduced proliferation of hormone-responsive breast tissue

choices.label: D
choices.text: Thickening of the cervical mucus blocking ascending infection

choices.label: E
choices.text: Thinning of the endometrium from the combined hormones

explanation.summary: Long-term combined OCP use lowers endometrial cancer rates, likely because of endometrial thinning.
explanation.whyCorrect: Long-term use of combined OCPs is associated with lower rates of endometrial cancer, likely due to endometrial thinning. Concurrent estrogen and progesterone suppress endometrial growth, which is also why these drugs treat abnormal uterine bleeding and dysmenorrhea.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Decreased ovulation is the mechanism proposed for the reduced risk of ovarian cancer, not endometrial cancer.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Lowered androgen synthesis explains the benefit in hyperandrogenism and acne, not endometrial cancer risk.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Hormonal contraceptives can increase proliferation of hormone-responsive tissue; this choice is neither accurate nor related to the endometrium.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Cervical mucus thickening is a contraceptive mechanism of progestin and is not the described basis of endometrial protection.

questions.stem: A 36-year-old woman considering combined oral contraceptive pills asks whether they will give her breast cancer, citing studies she read about an associated risk. Based on current research, which of the following is the most accurate counseling statement?

choices.label: A
choices.text: They cause new breast cancers only after more than 5 years of continuous use

choices.label: B
choices.text: They do not cause new cancers but may increase the growth rate of existing cancers

choices.label: C
choices.text: They have no effect of any kind on hormone-responsive tissues in the body

choices.label: D
choices.text: They lower breast cancer risk by suppressing ovulation over many cycles

choices.label: E
choices.text: They raise breast cancer risk only in women who smoke after age 35 years

explanation.summary: Current research indicates oral contraceptives do not cause new cancer but may accelerate the growth of existing hormone-responsive cancers.
explanation.whyCorrect: Although studies showing an increased breast cancer risk associated with OCP use prompted concern, current research indicates that oral contraceptives do not cause new cancer but may increase the growth rate of existing cancers, since hormonal contraceptives can increase proliferation of hormone-responsive tissue types. This is also why a history of breast cancer is an absolute contraindication.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The greater-than-5-years threshold applies to hepatocellular adenoma risk, and OCPs are not described as causing new breast cancers at any duration.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Hormonal contraceptives can increase proliferation of hormone-responsive tissue, so a claim of no effect is inaccurate.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Decreased ovulation underlies the reduced risk of ovarian cancer; OCPs are not described as protective against breast cancer.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Smoking after age 35 raises clotting risk with estrogen; it is not the determinant of the breast cancer relationship.

questions.stem: A 44-year-old woman who has used combined oral contraceptive pills for many years develops right upper quadrant pain after fatty meals, and ultrasonography shows gallstones. Which of the following effects of her contraceptive most likely contributed to this finding?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A hepatocellular adenoma is compressing the common bile duct

choices.label: B
choices.text: Estrogen and progesterone increase the risk of cholelithiasis

choices.label: C
choices.text: Increased coagulability caused thrombosis of the cystic artery

choices.label: D
choices.text: Progestin-mediated androgen receptor agonism altered the bile

choices.label: E
choices.text: Suppression of gonadotropins reduced gallbladder emptying

explanation.summary: Estrogen and progesterone are known to increase the risk of gallstones, which is why gallbladder disease is a relative contraindication to combined OCPs.
explanation.whyCorrect: Gallbladder disease is listed as a relative contraindication to combined oral contraceptives because estrogen and progesterone are known to increase the risk of gallstones. Long-term combined OCP use therefore plausibly contributed to this patient's cholelithiasis.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Estrogen-containing pills raise the risk of hepatocellular adenoma, but that is a benign liver tumor, not the described cause of gallstones.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Estrogen's increased coagulability manifests as DVT, pulmonary embolism, myocardial infarction, or stroke, not gallstone formation.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Androgen receptor agonism by some progestins explains weight gain, not stone formation in the gallbladder.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Gonadotropin suppression is the contraceptive mechanism; it is not the described link to gallstones.

questions.stem: A 19-year-old woman with polycystic ovary syndrome has acne, hirsutism, and irregular bleeding. She is started on a combined oral contraceptive, and over several months her acne and hirsutism improve. Which of the following best explains this improvement?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Decreased LH release by negative feedback lowers androgen synthesis

choices.label: B
choices.text: Estrogen thickens the cervical mucus and thins the endometrium

choices.label: C
choices.text: Increased FSH release accelerates maturation of ovarian follicles

choices.label: D
choices.text: Progestin directly blocks androgen receptors in the skin and hair

choices.label: E
choices.text: The hormones stimulate prolactin, which suppresses ovarian steroids

explanation.summary: Combined OCPs treat hyperandrogenism because estrogen and progestin decrease LH release by negative feedback, lowering androgen synthesis.
explanation.whyCorrect: Combined oral contraceptives treat hyperandrogenism because estrogen and progestin decrease LH release by negative feedback, which in turn lowers androgen synthesis. This decreases acne, a common virilizing effect of increased androgens, and in PCOS improves acne, hirsutism, and irregular bleeding.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Mucus thickening is a progestin effect and endometrial changes explain bleeding control, but neither lowers androgen production.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The pills suppress rather than increase gonadotropins; estrogen's key contraceptive action is FSH suppression, not stimulation.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The benefit comes from lowering androgen synthesis via reduced LH, not from receptor blockade in peripheral tissues.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Prolactin stimulation is not the described mechanism; the pathway runs through reduced LH and androgen synthesis.

questions.stem: A 31-year-old woman has disabling migraines that occur predictably around each menstrual period, without aura. She cannot take estrogen because of a prior deep vein thrombosis and requests contraception that is also most likely to improve her menstrual-related migraines. Which of the following methods is the best choice?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Copper-containing intrauterine device

choices.label: B
choices.text: Diaphragm used together with spermicide

choices.label: C
choices.text: Progestin-containing subdermal implant

choices.label: D
choices.text: Progestin-releasing intrauterine device

choices.label: E
choices.text: Traditional progestin-only contraceptive pill

explanation.summary: Among progestin-only methods, only those that reliably stop ovulation, such as the subdermal implant, improve PMDD, PMS symptoms, and menstrual-related migraines.
explanation.whyCorrect: Progestin-only options that stop ovulation can improve premenstrual dysphoric disorder, common PMS symptoms, and menstrual-related migraines. The subcutaneous implant reliably stops ovulation (as does the IM injection), so it addresses both her estrogen contraindication and her cycle-linked migraines.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The copper IUD is nonhormonal, has no effect on ovulation, and can increase cramping and bleeding; it offers no benefit for her migraines.
whyWrongByChoice.B: A diaphragm with spermicide is a barrier method with a 12% pregnancy rate and no influence on the hormonal cycle driving her symptoms.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The progestin IUD avoids estrogen but is not among the progestin-only options that reliably stop ovulation, the property needed to improve menstrual-related migraines.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The traditional progestin-only pill works primarily by thickening cervical mucus and does not reliably stop ovulation, so it would not target her cycle-related symptoms.

questions.stem: A 24-year-old woman who cannot take estrogen wants an oral contraceptive, but her work schedule makes taking a pill at exactly the same time every day difficult. Her physician prescribes the newer progestin-only pill Slynd rather than a traditional minipill. Compared with the traditional minipill, which of the following is an advantage of this drug?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It adds protection against sexually transmitted infections

choices.label: B
choices.text: It contains a low estrogen dose that stabilizes the uterine lining

choices.label: C
choices.text: It must be taken within the same 4 to 6 hour window every day

choices.label: D
choices.text: It reliably stops ovulation and allows a much wider dosing window

choices.label: E
choices.text: It works by creating a sperm-toxic inflammatory uterine environment

explanation.summary: Slynd widened the dosing window and reliably stops ovulation in addition to thickening cervical mucus, making it more effective and more forgiving than the traditional minipill.
explanation.whyCorrect: Slynd, a progestin-only pill marketed in 2019, widened the dosing window significantly, making adherence easier. It also reliably stops ovulation, like a combined OCP, while still thickening cervical mucus like other progestin-only options, which makes it more effective than the traditional minipill.

whyWrongByChoice.A: No pill protects against sexually transmitted infections; condoms provide STI protection.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Slynd is a progestin-only pill; it contains no estrogen, which is why it suits a patient who cannot take estrogen.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Strict timing, where even a 4 to 6 hour delay mid-cycle can cause failure, is the limitation of the traditional minipill that Slynd was designed to overcome.
whyWrongByChoice.E: A sperm-toxic inflammatory uterine environment is the mechanism of the copper IUD, not of any progestin pill.

questions.stem: A 26-year-old woman had a progestin-containing subdermal implant placed 8 months ago. Her menstrual bleeding has now stopped entirely, and she is worried something is wrong. A urine pregnancy test is negative. Which of the following is the most appropriate response?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Absent menses after implant placement indicates ovarian failure

choices.label: B
choices.text: Absent menses indicates the implant has stopped releasing hormone

choices.label: C
choices.text: Missed periods caused by the contraceptive do not cause physiologic problems

choices.label: D
choices.text: She should add a combined pill to bring back monthly bleeding

choices.label: E
choices.text: The implant should be removed immediately to restore her cycles

explanation.summary: Progestin-only methods can stop monthly bleeding entirely, and missed periods due to contraception cause no physiologic problems.
explanation.whyCorrect: Progestin-only birth control usually decreases menstrual bleeding and can cause irregular spotting in the first months; for some patients monthly bleeding stops entirely. Missed periods due to contraception do not cause any physiologic problems, so reassurance is appropriate.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Contraceptive amenorrhea reflects the progestin's effects, not loss of ovarian function.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Amenorrhea is an expected effect of progestin-only methods, not a sign of device failure; the implant remains effective for 5 years.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Adding estrogen-containing pills to force monthly bleeding is not indicated, since the amenorrhea is not harmful.
whyWrongByChoice.E: There is no indication for removal; the absent bleeding is a recognized, harmless effect of the method.

questions.stem: A 30-year-old woman receiving depot medroxyprogesterone injections every 12 weeks reports steady weight gain since starting the method. Which of the following pharmacologic properties best explains this adverse effect?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Agonism of androgen receptors by the progestin

choices.label: B
choices.text: Blockade of prolactin's effect on milk synthesis

choices.label: C
choices.text: Estrogen-mediated retention of sodium and water

choices.label: D
choices.text: Local inflammation at the intramuscular injection site

choices.label: E
choices.text: Suppression of gonadotropin-releasing hormone release

explanation.summary: Injectable medroxyprogesterone causes weight gain in some patients, as can any progestin with androgen receptor agonism.
explanation.whyCorrect: Injectable medroxyprogesterone is known to cause weight gain in some patients, as can any form of progestin with androgen receptor agonism; individual sensitivity varies.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Progesterone's blockade of prolactin's effect on milk synthesis matters for timing contraception in breastfeeding, not for weight gain.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The injection is progestin-only; there is no estrogen component to cause the effect.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Injection-site inflammation is not the described basis of the weight gain seen with this drug.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Central suppression of gonadotropins is how hormonal methods prevent ovulation; it is not the property tied to weight gain.

questions.stem: A 28-year-old woman wants effective contraception for about the next year but hopes to become pregnant promptly after stopping. Which of the following methods is LEAST appropriate for her, given its effect on the return of fertility after discontinuation?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Combined oral contraceptive pills

choices.label: B
choices.text: Copper-containing intrauterine device

choices.label: C
choices.text: Progesterone intramuscular injection

choices.label: D
choices.text: Progesterone subcutaneous implant

choices.label: E
choices.text: Progestin-containing intrauterine device

explanation.summary: The medroxyprogesterone injection is associated with a delay in the ability to become pregnant after stopping, unlike the other reversible methods.
explanation.whyCorrect: Among the disadvantages of the progesterone intramuscular injection are possible weight gain, hair or skin changes, reversible bone density loss, and a delay in the ability to become pregnant after stopping. For a patient who wants to conceive promptly after discontinuing contraception, this delay makes the injection the least suitable choice.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Oral pills require daily adherence but are not associated with a delay in conceiving after they are stopped.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The copper IUD is reversible; its drawbacks are possible increased cramping and bleeding, not delayed fertility.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The implant is reversible with irregular bleeding as its main drawback; no post-removal fertility delay is described.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The progestin IUD is reversible and is not described as delaying the return of fertility after removal.

questions.stem: A 38-year-old man whose family is complete asks about vasectomy. Which of the following counseling statements about this procedure is most accurate?

choices.label: A
choices.text: If it is later reversed, return of fertility is highly variable, from 30% to 80%

choices.label: B
choices.text: It has a higher pregnancy rate after the procedure than female tubal ligation does

choices.label: C
choices.text: It provides reliable protection against sexually transmitted infections

choices.label: D
choices.text: It restores full fertility in nearly all men who undergo reversal surgery

choices.label: E
choices.text: It stops the testes from producing sperm within several weeks of surgery

explanation.summary: Vasectomy is highly effective (0.15% pregnancy rate) and permanent, and fertility after reversal is highly variable, from 30% to 80%.
explanation.whyCorrect: Vasectomy blocks sperm transport by ligating the ductus deferens and has a pregnancy rate of about 0.15%, lower than tubal ligation's 0.5%. Although reversal is possible, fertility after vasectomy reversal is highly variable, ranging from 30% to 80%, and sterilization can permanently block fertility even after reversal surgery.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Vasectomy's pregnancy rate is about 0.15%, lower than the 0.5% rate of tubal ligation.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Sterilization offers no STI protection; condoms are the methods that protect against sexually transmitted infections.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Reversal outcomes are highly variable, and sterilization can permanently block fertility even after reversal surgery.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Vasectomy prevents transport of sperm from the testes to the urethra; it does not stop sperm production.

questions.stem: A 33-year-old woman with two children conceives while using the contraceptive sponge. She used the same method successfully for several years before her children were born and is surprised by its failure. Which of the following best explains her contraceptive failure?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The sponge contains hormones that become ineffective with repeated use

choices.label: B
choices.text: The sponge is effective only when inserted immediately before intercourse

choices.label: C
choices.text: The sponge is substantially less effective in women who have had children

choices.label: D
choices.text: The sponge loses potency unless it is replaced every day of the cycle

choices.label: E
choices.text: The sponge requires a new fitting by a provider after each pregnancy

explanation.summary: The contraceptive sponge is less effective after childbirth, with a pregnancy rate of 24% in parous women versus 12% in nulliparous women.
explanation.whyCorrect: The sponge's pregnancy rate is 24% in parous women compared with 12% in nulliparous women; being less effective after having children is a listed disadvantage of the method. Her failure risk roughly doubled after her deliveries even with the same use pattern.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The sponge is a nonhormonal method; one of its listed advantages is having no hormone effects.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The sponge can be inserted up to a day before intercourse; last-minute insertion is not required.
whyWrongByChoice.D: No daily replacement schedule is described for the sponge; its parity-dependent efficacy explains the failure.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Fitting by a provider is a feature of the cervical cap and diaphragm, not the sponge.

questions.stem: A 25-year-old woman with a latex allergy has a new partner and wants a contraceptive method she can use herself that also protects against sexually transmitted infections. Which of the following methods best meets both requirements?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Copper-containing intrauterine device

choices.label: B
choices.text: Diaphragm used with spermicide

choices.label: C
choices.text: Female (internal) condom

choices.label: D
choices.text: Male latex condom

choices.label: E
choices.text: Withdrawal before ejaculation

explanation.summary: The female (internal) condom provides STI protection and may be used by those with latex allergy.
explanation.whyCorrect: The female condom is a pouch inserted in the vagina to catch ejaculated semen. Its listed advantages include use by those with latex allergy, compatibility with breastfeeding, and STI protection, making it the barrier option she can use herself despite her allergy.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The copper IUD is highly effective contraception but provides no STI protection.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The diaphragm protects against some infections but is not listed as providing STI protection and carries a bladder infection risk.
whyWrongByChoice.D: A male latex condom protects against STIs but is unsuitable given her latex allergy, and it is used by the partner.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Withdrawal provides no STI protection and fails if performed too late, with a 22% pregnancy rate.

questions.stem: A 24-year-old woman with a body mass index of 31 requests emergency contraception 20 hours after unprotected intercourse. She obtains levonorgestrel (Plan B) over the counter and takes it immediately. Which of the following features of this case most reduces the likelihood that the medication will prevent pregnancy?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Her body mass index greater than 25

choices.label: B
choices.text: Obtaining the drug without a prescription

choices.label: C
choices.text: Taking the dose before ovulation occurred

choices.label: D
choices.text: The 20-hour interval since intercourse

choices.label: E
choices.text: Using a levonorgestrel-based formulation

explanation.summary: Levonorgestrel emergency contraception is less effective in women with a body mass index greater than 25.
explanation.whyCorrect: A listed disadvantage of the levonorgestrel emergency contraceptive pill is that it is less effective in females with a body mass index greater than 25. Her timing is actually favorable: used within 24 hours, the pregnancy rate is 5%, compared with 15% within 48 hours and 50% within 72 hours.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Levonorgestrel is usually available over the counter; this is an advantage of the method, not a limitation.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Hormonal emergency contraception works by preventing or delaying ovulation, so use before ovulation is when it works best.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Taking the pill within 24 hours is the most effective window, with a pregnancy rate of about 5%.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Levonorgestrel is an appropriate emergency contraceptive within 3 days of unprotected sex; the formulation itself is not the problem here.

questions.stem: A 28-year-old woman requests emergency contraception 2 days after unprotected intercourse. Basal body temperature and urinary hormone tracking indicate that she ovulated the day before the encounter. She is counseled that hormonal emergency contraception may not work well in her situation. Which of the following best explains this counseling?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Hormonal emergency contraception acts mainly by preventing or delaying ovulation

choices.label: B
choices.text: Hormonal emergency contraception is effective only within 12 hours of intercourse

choices.label: C
choices.text: Hormonal emergency contraception permanently suppresses future ovulatory cycles

choices.label: D
choices.text: Hormonal emergency contraception requires a copper device to be effective

choices.label: E
choices.text: Hormonal emergency contraception works by terminating an established pregnancy

explanation.summary: Hormonal emergency contraception prevents or delays ovulation when taken before ovulation, so it is less effective once ovulation has already occurred.
explanation.whyCorrect: The mechanism of hormonal emergency contraception is to prevent or delay ovulation if used prior to ovulation. If ovulation has already occurred, as in this patient, emergency contraception may not be as effective. It decreases the chance of implantation but cannot eliminate the pregnancy risk, which ranges from 0% to 30% per act depending on cycle day.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Emergency contraception methods can work for up to 5 days after unprotected intercourse, not just 12 hours.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Emergency contraception affects the current cycle; it does not permanently suppress ovulation.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The hormonal pills act on their own; no copper device is part of their mechanism.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Emergency contraception decreases the chance of implantation occurring; it does not terminate an established pregnancy.

questions.stem: A 29-year-old woman whose menstrual cycles vary unpredictably from 24 to 38 days asks about using natural family planning (the rhythm method) as her only contraception. Which of the following is the most important counseling point for this patient?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The method cannot be combined with barrier methods on fertile days

choices.label: B
choices.text: The method has a pregnancy rate below 1% with typical use

choices.label: C
choices.text: The method is not effective for women with irregular periods

choices.label: D
choices.text: The method provides reliable protection against infections

choices.label: E
choices.text: The method requires fitting and placement by a provider

explanation.summary: Natural family planning is not effective with irregular periods and requires regular monitoring and tracking of fertility signs.
explanation.whyCorrect: Fertility awareness-based methods identify the fertile window through observation of cycle length, basal body temperature, urinary hormone measurement, and cervical mucus, and they require daily observation. A listed disadvantage is that the rhythm method is not effective during fertile days or with irregular periods, which directly applies to this patient's unpredictable 24- to 38-day cycles.

whyWrongByChoice.A: These methods explicitly pair with abstinence or barrier method use on fertile days, so combining them is expected, not prohibited.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Natural family planning carries a pregnancy rate of about 24%, among the highest of the listed methods.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The rhythm method provides no STI protection.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Provider fitting applies to the cervical cap and diaphragm; the rhythm method involves tracking fertility signs, not a fitted device.

questions.stem: A 31-year-old woman has had three episodes of acute cystitis in the 6 months since she began using a new contraceptive method. She reports that the method must be fitted, is placed to cover the cervix before intercourse, and must be used with spermicide. Which of the following methods is she most likely using?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Contraceptive sponge

choices.label: B
choices.text: Copper intrauterine device

choices.label: C
choices.text: Diaphragm

choices.label: D
choices.text: Female (internal) condom

choices.label: E
choices.text: Vaginal ring

explanation.summary: The diaphragm is a fitted cervical barrier that must be used with spermicide and carries a risk of bladder infection.
explanation.whyCorrect: The diaphragm is a physical barrier that covers the cervix, preventing sperm from entering the uterus, and it requires fitting and proper placement. Its listed disadvantages include the need for spermicide, unsuitability during vaginal infection or bleeding, a 12% pregnancy rate, and a risk of bladder infection, which fits her recurrent cystitis.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The sponge needs no fitting, and its drawbacks are irritation, reduced efficacy after childbirth, and being unsafe during menses, not bladder infection.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The copper IUD is placed by a provider inside the uterus; its issues are cramping, bleeding, and rare uterine injury, not bladder infection.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The female condom is an inserted pouch that requires no fitting or spermicide; it may slip out of place but is not linked to cystitis.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The vaginal ring is a hormonal method that does not need to be custom fitted and requires no spermicide; its drawbacks are discharge and spotting.

questions.stem: A 26-year-old woman comes to the office for her postpartum visit 6 weeks after an uncomplicated vaginal delivery of a healthy term infant. She and her husband would like more children and ask how long they should wait before conceiving again. Which of the following intervals from this delivery to conception of the next pregnancy is associated with the lowest risk of preterm birth, low birthweight, and small-for-gestational-age birth?

choices.label: A
choices.text: 6 to 11 months

choices.label: B
choices.text: Less than 6 months

choices.label: C
choices.text: 12 to 17 months

choices.label: D
choices.text: 18 to 23 months

choices.label: E
choices.text: 36 months or longer

explanation.summary: An interpregnancy interval of 18-23 months appears optimal for minimizing adverse neonatal outcomes.
explanation.whyCorrect: The interpregnancy interval is a modifiable risk factor that should be addressed in prenatal and postpartum counseling. Intervals of 18-23 months are associated with the lowest risk of preterm birth, low birthweight, and small-for-gestational-age birth.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Patients should be counseled about the risks and benefits of repeat pregnancy sooner than 18 months; this interval is not the stated optimum.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Intervals shorter than 6 months should be avoided because they increase the odds of preterm birth, low birthweight, and small-for-gestational-age birth.
whyWrongByChoice.C: This interval is still shorter than 18 months, the threshold below which counseling about added risk is recommended.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Very long intervals are not identified as the optimal window; 18-23 months is the interval described as minimizing risk.

questions.topicName: Family Planning, Preconception Care and Infertility

questions.stem: A 24-year-old woman comes to the office for an annual health maintenance visit. As part of routine screening, the physician asks, "Would you like to become pregnant in the next year?" The patient pauses and says she honestly is not sure. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Begin preconception screening for modifiable risk factors

choices.label: B
choices.text: Defer the topic until she has made a decision

choices.label: C
choices.text: Discuss her goals, priorities, resources, and values

choices.label: D
choices.text: Prescribe a combined oral contraceptive today

choices.label: E
choices.text: Schedule placement of a subdermal contraceptive implant

explanation.summary: Patients who are unsure about pregnancy intention warrant further discussion of their goals, priorities, resources, and values.
explanation.whyCorrect: Pregnancy intention screening tailors counseling to the response: "yes" leads to preconception counseling, "no" leads to an offer of contraceptive options, and an unsure answer calls for further exploration of the patient's goals, priorities, resources, and values.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Preconception counseling and screening for modifiable risk factors is the pathway for patients who answer "yes," not for those who are undecided.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Deferring misses the opportunity this screening is designed to create; the unsure response itself is the trigger for further discussion now.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Offering evidence-based contraception is the response for patients who answer "no"; prescribing before exploring her goals skips the indicated discussion.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Committing her to a long-acting method presumes she does not want pregnancy, which she has not said; her goals should be clarified first.

questions.topicName: Family Planning, Preconception Care and Infertility

questions.stem: A 19-year-old nulliparous college student comes to the clinic requesting contraception. She wants the most effective reversible method available but says a friend told her that intrauterine and implanted devices are only for women who have already had children. She has no chronic medical conditions. Which of the following is the most appropriate response?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Barrier methods offer efficacy equivalent to intrauterine devices when used consistently

choices.label: B
choices.text: Combined oral contraceptive pills are the most effective reversible option available to her

choices.label: C
choices.text: Her friend is correct, so depot medroxyprogesterone injections are her best option

choices.label: D
choices.text: Long-acting reversible contraceptives are suitable for her and have a failure rate below 1% per year

choices.label: E
choices.text: Permanent sterilization is the only method with a failure rate below 1% per year

explanation.summary: LARCs are Tier I methods with a failure rate under 1% per year and are appropriate for nulliparous women and adolescents.
explanation.whyCorrect: Long-acting reversible contraceptives, including IUDs and subdermal implants, are recommended for their high efficacy and convenience and are suitable for most females, explicitly including nulliparous females and adolescents. They sit in Tier I with a failure rate of less than 1% per year.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Barrier methods are Tier III, with an 18-28% failure rate per year, far below IUD effectiveness.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Combined hormonal contraceptives are Tier II methods with a 6-12% failure rate per year, less effective than LARCs.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The friend's claim is incorrect; LARCs are suitable for nulliparous women, and depot medroxyprogesterone is a Tier II method.
whyWrongByChoice.E: LARCs share Tier I status with permanent sterilization, and unlike sterilization they are reversible, which matches her request.

questions.topicName: Family Planning, Preconception Care and Infertility

questions.stem: A 31-year-old woman comes to the clinic requesting the combined estrogen-progestin oral contraceptive pill that her sister uses. Her history is notable for occasional wine with dinner, a BMI of 32 kg/m2, chlamydia treated 3 years ago, and recurrent headaches preceded by 20 minutes of shimmering zigzag lines in her vision. She has never been pregnant. Which of the following features of her history contraindicates the requested method?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Body mass index of 32 kg/m2

choices.label: B
choices.text: Headaches preceded by visual aura

choices.label: C
choices.text: Nulliparity

choices.label: D
choices.text: Occasional alcohol consumption

choices.label: E
choices.text: Previously treated chlamydia infection

explanation.summary: Migraine with aura contraindicates estrogen-containing combined hormonal contraceptives.
explanation.whyCorrect: Combined hormonal contraceptives containing estrogen are contraindicated in females with certain conditions, including migraine with aura, uncontrolled hypertension, a history of venous thromboembolism, and active liver disease. Her stereotyped visual aura preceding headaches places her in this group.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Elevated BMI is a target for preconception weight counseling but is not listed among the contraindications to estrogen-containing contraception.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Nulliparity does not restrict contraceptive choice; even LARCs are suitable for nulliparous females.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Occasional alcohol use is a lifestyle factor addressed in preconception counseling; it does not contraindicate combined contraceptives.
whyWrongByChoice.E: A remote, treated sexually transmitted infection is relevant to STI screening, not to eligibility for combined hormonal methods.

questions.topicName: Family Planning, Preconception Care and Infertility

questions.stem: A 27-year-old woman comes to the office for a preconception visit. She and her partner plan to begin trying to conceive soon. Prenatal laboratory screening shows she is nonimmune to rubella. Which of the following is the most appropriate management?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Administer MMR today and advise avoiding pregnancy for at least 1 month

choices.label: B
choices.text: Administer MMR today and advise avoiding pregnancy for at least 12 months

choices.label: C
choices.text: Administer MMR today and advise that she may begin trying to conceive immediately

choices.label: D
choices.text: Defer MMR until the postpartum period after her next delivery

choices.label: E
choices.text: Defer MMR until the second trimester of the anticipated pregnancy

explanation.summary: Live attenuated vaccines such as MMR should be given preconceptionally, with pregnancy avoided for at least 1 month afterward.
explanation.whyCorrect: Live attenuated vaccines, including MMR and varicella, are contraindicated during pregnancy because of the theoretical risk of fetal infection and should be administered before conception. It is recommended to avoid pregnancy for at least 1 month after vaccination; ACIP specifies 28 days after each dose of a live vaccine.

whyWrongByChoice.B: A 12-month delay far exceeds the recommended interval; only about 1 month of pregnancy avoidance is advised after MMR.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Conceiving immediately ignores the recommended waiting period of at least 1 month (28 days) after a live vaccine.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Waiting until postpartum leaves her nonimmune through the pregnancy; the vaccine should be given preconceptionally at this visit.
whyWrongByChoice.E: MMR is a live attenuated vaccine and is contraindicated at any point during pregnancy.

questions.topicName: Family Planning, Preconception Care and Infertility

questions.stem: A 30-year-old woman comes to the office because she and her husband plan to begin trying to conceive in 3 months. She asks whether she should take any supplements beforehand. Which of the following regimens is most appropriate to reduce the risk of neural tube defects?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Folic acid 40 mcg daily, beginning at least 1 month before conception

choices.label: B
choices.text: Folic acid 400-800 mcg daily, beginning after the first positive pregnancy test

choices.label: C
choices.text: Folic acid 400-800 mcg daily, beginning at least 1 month before conception

choices.label: D
choices.text: Folic acid 400-800 mcg daily, beginning in the second trimester

choices.label: E
choices.text: Folic acid 400-800 mcg once weekly, beginning at least 1 month before conception

explanation.summary: Folic acid 400-800 mcg daily, started at least 1 month before conception and continued through early pregnancy, reduces neural tube defect risk.
explanation.whyCorrect: Nutritional optimization is a core component of preconception care, and folic acid supplementation of 400-800 mcg daily started at least one month before conception and continued through early pregnancy significantly reduces the risk of neural tube defects.

whyWrongByChoice.A: 40 mcg is one-tenth of the lower end of the recommended 400-800 mcg daily dose.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Starting only after a positive test misses the preconception month of supplementation that the recommendation specifies.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The protective window is preconception through early pregnancy; the second trimester is too late to start.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The recommended dosing is daily, not weekly.

questions.topicName: Family Planning, Preconception Care and Infertility

questions.stem: A 28-year-old woman with epilepsy that has been well controlled on valproate for 4 years comes to the office because she plans to conceive in about 6 months. She takes no other medications. In addition to starting folic acid, which of the following is the most appropriate management of her antiepileptic therapy?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Continue valproate and switch only after pregnancy is confirmed

choices.label: B
choices.text: Continue valproate unchanged because her seizures are controlled

choices.label: C
choices.text: Discontinue valproate now without a replacement agent

choices.label: D
choices.text: Reduce the valproate dose by half once she conceives

choices.label: E
choices.text: Substitute a safer alternative antiepileptic before conception

explanation.summary: Potentially teratogenic medications such as valproate should be identified and substituted with safer alternatives before conception.
explanation.whyCorrect: Comprehensive medication review is essential in preconception care to identify and modify potentially teratogenic medications. Certain antiepileptic drugs such as valproate may need to be substituted with safer alternatives before conception, making a planned preconception switch the correct strategy.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Waiting until pregnancy is confirmed exposes the early embryo to the teratogen during the window preconception care is designed to protect.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Seizure control does not remove the teratogenic risk; the point of the preconception visit is to modify such medications ahead of pregnancy.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Stopping her antiepileptic without a replacement leaves her epilepsy untreated; the recommendation is substitution, not abrupt discontinuation.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Halving the dose after conception is not a described strategy; the medication should be replaced before conception.

questions.topicName: Family Planning, Preconception Care and Infertility

questions.stem: A primary care practice is designing a protocol for intimate partner violence screening at preconception visits. Which of the following elements is most appropriate to include?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Informing patients of mandatory state reporting requirements before screening

choices.label: B
choices.text: Prioritizing screening for patients of lower socioeconomic status

choices.label: C
choices.text: Promising absolute confidentiality regardless of what is disclosed

choices.label: D
choices.text: Requiring physician interviews because questionnaires are unreliable

choices.label: E
choices.text: Restricting screening to patients with visible signs of injury

explanation.summary: Before IPV screening, clinicians must inform patients about mandatory reporting requirements under state law.
explanation.whyCorrect: IPV screening should be framed as universal for all patients in the practice, using validated tools with adequate sensitivity and specificity. While privacy and confidentiality assurances matter, clinicians must inform patients about mandatory reporting requirements under state law before screening.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Psychosocial screening should be performed for all females seeking pregnancy evaluation regardless of social status, educational level, race, or ethnicity.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Absolute confidentiality cannot be promised because state mandatory reporting laws may require disclosure.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Self-administered questionnaires are as effective as physician interviews for IPV screening.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Screening should be universal at preconception counseling, not limited to patients with apparent injuries.

questions.topicName: Family Planning, Preconception Care and Infertility

questions.stem: A 36-year-old woman and her 34-year-old husband come to the office because they have not conceived after 6 months of regular, unprotected intercourse. Her menstrual cycles occur every 28 days, and neither partner has a significant medical history. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Begin empiric letrozole without further evaluation

choices.label: B
choices.text: Evaluate the female partner only, since her age is the concern

choices.label: C
choices.text: Initiate infertility evaluation of both partners now

choices.label: D
choices.text: Reassure the couple and reassess after 12 total months of trying

choices.label: E
choices.text: Refer the couple directly for in vitro fertilization

explanation.summary: When the female partner is 35 or older, infertility evaluation should begin after 6 months rather than the standard 12 months.
explanation.whyCorrect: Infertility is defined as failure to achieve pregnancy after 12 months of regular, unprotected intercourse, but evaluation is initiated earlier when the female partner is 35 years or older, when risk factors for infertility exist, or in nonheterosexual partnerships. At 36, this patient qualifies for evaluation after 6 months, and workup should include both partners.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Ovulation induction is first-line for anovulatory infertility, but she has regular cycles and no evaluation has established a cause.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Male factor is one of the three most common identifiable causes of infertility, so a semen analysis for the husband belongs in the initial workup.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Waiting for the 12-month definition applies to women younger than 35; her age moves the threshold to 6 months.
whyWrongByChoice.E: IVF is the most effective treatment, but jumping there before any evaluation skips the indicated workup of both partners.

questions.topicName: Family Planning, Preconception Care and Infertility

questions.stem: A 33-year-old man is evaluated for infertility. Two semen analyses obtained one month apart both show a complete absence of sperm in the ejaculate. Physical examination shows normal testes and a palpable vas deferens bilaterally. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A third semen analysis in one month

choices.label: B
choices.text: Empiric exogenous testosterone therapy

choices.label: C
choices.text: Genetic testing for cystic fibrosis

choices.label: D
