whyWrongByChoice.D: The pelvic splanchnic nerves carry sacral parasympathetic fibers mediating reflexogenic arousal, erectile tissue engorgement, and vaginal lubrication, not skeletal muscle expulsion.

questions.stem: Sperm are produced in the testes and ultimately expelled from the body during ejaculation. Which of the following is the correct order of structures that sperm pass through during emission and ejaculation?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Epididymis, seminiferous tubules, ejaculatory ducts, vas deferens, urethra

choices.label: B
choices.text: Seminiferous tubules, ejaculatory ducts, epididymis, vas deferens, urethra

choices.label: C
choices.text: Seminiferous tubules, epididymis, ejaculatory ducts, vas deferens, urethra

choices.label: D
choices.text: Seminiferous tubules, epididymis, vas deferens, ejaculatory ducts, urethra

choices.label: E
choices.text: Seminiferous tubules, vas deferens, epididymis, ejaculatory ducts, urethra

explanation.summary: The SEVEN UP mnemonic gives the sperm pathway: Seminiferous tubules, Epididymis, Vas deferens, Ejaculatory ducts, (Nothing), Urethra, Penis.
explanation.whyCorrect: Sperm are produced in the seminiferous tubules of the testes, stored in the epididymis, and move through the ductus (vas) deferens and ejaculatory ducts into the urethra, exiting via the penis. The mnemonic SEVEN UP captures this order: Seminiferous tubules, Epididymis, Vas deferens, Ejaculatory ducts, (Nothing), Urethra, Penis.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Sperm originate in the seminiferous tubules, not the epididymis, and the vas deferens precedes the ejaculatory ducts.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The epididymis immediately follows the seminiferous tubules; the ejaculatory ducts come after the vas deferens, not before the epididymis.
whyWrongByChoice.C: This reverses the ejaculatory ducts and vas deferens; sperm travel through the vas deferens before the ejaculatory ducts.
whyWrongByChoice.E: This places the vas deferens before the epididymis; sperm are stored in the epididymis before entering the vas deferens.

questions.stem: A biochemical analysis of a semen sample identifies fructose, citric acid, and lipids contributed by the seminal vesicles, prostate, and other accessory glands. Which of the following is the primary role of these particular components?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Liquefying the coagulated semen after ejaculation

choices.label: B
choices.text: Lubricating the urethra during semen passage

choices.label: C
choices.text: Providing antimicrobial protection for the urethra

choices.label: D
choices.text: Reducing vaginal acidity to support sperm survival

choices.label: E
choices.text: Serving as energy sources for the sperm

explanation.summary: The fructose, citric acid, and lipids in seminal fluid serve as energy sources for sperm.
explanation.whyCorrect: Seminal fluid contains sperm along with secretions from the seminal vesicles, prostate gland, and bulbourethral glands. Among these secretions, fructose, citric acid, and lipids serve as energy sources for sperm, supporting them as they travel through the female reproductive tract toward the uterine (fallopian) tubes where fertilization typically occurs.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Liquefaction of semen is the job of the proteolytic enzymes in the accessory gland secretions, not the fructose, citric acid, and lipids.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Lubrication is provided by the mucus component of the secretions, not by the energy substrates.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Antimicrobial protection of the urethra is the proposed role of the paraurethral (Skene's) gland fluid in females, not of these seminal energy substrates.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Reducing vaginal acidity is a function of vaginal lubrication, the neurogenic plasma transudate produced during female arousal, not of these semen components.

questions.stem: During female sexual arousal, a fluid appears in the vagina that is a neurogenic plasma transudate driven by increased capillary pressure during genital vasocongestion. Which of the following best describes how this fluid aids reproductive function?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It contains prostate-specific antigen that protects the urethra

choices.label: B
choices.text: It increases vaginal acidity to suppress competing microbes

choices.label: C
choices.text: It is secreted by the paraurethral glands at the moment of orgasm

choices.label: D
choices.text: It reduces vaginal acidity and raises oxygen tension for sperm

choices.label: E
choices.text: It supplies fructose and citric acid as energy substrates for sperm

explanation.summary: Vaginal lubrication reduces vaginal acidity and increases vaginal oxygen tension to support spermatozoal function.
explanation.whyCorrect: Vaginal lubrication is a neurogenic plasma transudate driven by increased capillary pressure during genital vasocongestion. It aids reproductive function by reducing vaginal acidity and increasing vaginal oxygen tension to support spermatozoal function, and it is distinctly different from female ejaculation.

whyWrongByChoice.A: PSA-containing fluid that may protect the urethra from microbes describes true female ejaculate from the paraurethral (Skene's) glands, not lubrication.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The transudate reduces vaginal acidity rather than increasing it; lower acidity supports sperm function.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The paraurethral (Skene's) glands produce the small-volume, thick, milky ejaculate; lubrication arises from capillary transudation during vasocongestion, not from these glands.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Fructose and citric acid are energy sources contributed to semen by the male accessory glands, not components of the vaginal transudate.

questions.stem: A physiology student observes that although clitoral erectile tissue engorges through the same NO-cGMP pathway as the penis, clitoral enlargement does not achieve the same rigidity as a penile erection. Which of the following structural differences best explains this observation?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Absence of endothelium-lined lacunar spaces in the erectile tissue

choices.label: B
choices.text: Absence of trabecular smooth muscle within the clitoral corpora

choices.label: C
choices.text: Inability of nitric oxide to relax clitoral vascular smooth muscle

choices.label: D
choices.text: Lack of ischiocavernosus muscles around the clitoral crura

choices.label: E
choices.text: Thinner tunica albuginea and no compressible venous plexus layer

explanation.summary: Clitoral engorgement is less rigid because the clitoral tunica albuginea is thinner and a compressible venous plexus layer is absent.
explanation.whyCorrect: The clitoral corpora cavernosa are surrounded by a tunica albuginea that is thinner than that of the penis, which contributes to the less rigid nature of clitoral engorgement. The reduced rigidity is also attributed to the possible absence of a compressible venous plexus layer, so the veno-occlusive trapping that raises penile pressure toward systolic levels is less effective.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Clitoral erectile tissue is composed of endothelial-lined lacunar spaces; these are present, not absent.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The clitoral corpora cavernosa, like those of the penis, contain trabecular smooth muscle along with endothelial-lined lacunar spaces and connective tissue.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Clitoral and labial engorgement is mediated by the same NO-cGMP pathway as penile erection, so NO acts normally on this tissue.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Ischiocavernosus muscles do surround the clitoral crura and help compress venous outflow, contributing to blood retention and engorgement.

questions.stem: A 26-year-old uncircumcised man reports pain during sex and when his foreskin is withdrawn while applying a condom. Examination shows several small tears in the foreskin with no discharge, ulcers, or other lesions, and testing for sexually transmitted infections is negative. Which of the following is the most appropriate management?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Collagenase injection therapy

choices.label: B
choices.text: Daily oral SSRI therapy

choices.label: C
choices.text: Empiric antibiotic therapy for gonorrhea and chlamydia

choices.label: D
choices.text: Intracavernosal phenylephrine injection

choices.label: E
choices.text: Preputioplasty without circumcision

explanation.summary: Painful sex from a tight foreskin with small tears may respond to small surgical incisions, not necessarily circumcision.
explanation.whyCorrect: Male dyspareunia is most often due to sexually transmitted or other genital infections, but some males with tight foreskins experience pain when the foreskin is withdrawn during condom application or sex. The resulting small tears in the foreskin may respond to small surgical incisions, which do not necessarily require circumcision.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Collagenase breaks down the fibrous plaques of Peyronie disease, which presents with penile curvature and painful erections, not foreskin tears.
whyWrongByChoice.B: SSRIs delay ejaculation and are first-line for premature ejaculation; they do not address foreskin tears.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Infection is the most common cause of male dyspareunia, but his STI testing is negative and the examination shows a mechanical foreskin problem, so empiric antibiotics are not indicated.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Intracavernosal phenylephrine is a treatment for ischemic priapism, a sustained painful erection lasting more than 4 hours, which he does not have.

questions.stem: A 31-year-old woman is brought to the clinic by her partner, who is upset that she wants sex less often than he does. She reports regular erotic thoughts, becomes aroused in response to cues, enjoys sexual activity when it occurs, sometimes initiates it, and feels no personal distress about her sexuality. Which of the following statements about a diagnosis of female sexual interest/arousal disorder (FSIAD) is most accurate?

choices.label: A
choices.text: She does not meet criteria for FSIAD; a desire discrepancy alone is insufficient

choices.label: B
choices.text: She meets criteria for female orgasmic disorder

choices.label: C
choices.text: She meets criteria for FSIAD and should start daily flibanserin

choices.label: D
choices.text: She meets criteria for FSIAD, and couples therapy is first line

choices.label: E
choices.text: She meets criteria for genito-pelvic pain/penetration disorder

explanation.summary: A desire discrepancy with a partner alone is insufficient for a diagnosis of FSIAD, which also requires indicator loss, duration, and clinically significant distress.
explanation.whyCorrect: FSIAD requires absence or reduction of at least 3 of the 6 indicators for at least 6 months and must cause clinically significant distress. A desire discrepancy, meaning lower desire than a partner, is alone insufficient for the diagnosis. She retains erotic thoughts, arousal to cues, pleasure, and initiation, and she has no personal distress, so no sexual dysfunction diagnosis applies.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Female orgasmic disorder involves absent, delayed, or reduced orgasm in at least 75% of encounters for at least 6 months with distress; she enjoys sexual activity and reports no such problem.
whyWrongByChoice.C: She does not meet FSIAD criteria, and even in FSIAD, psychological interventions are first line, with flibanserin only a medication option.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The premise is wrong: she does not meet FSIAD criteria, because a partner desire discrepancy alone is insufficient and she lacks clinically significant distress.
whyWrongByChoice.E: GPPPD requires difficulty with penetration, vulvovaginal or pelvic pain, fear or anxiety about pain, or pelvic floor tensing, none of which she reports.

questions.stem: A 52-year-old man with heart failure and hypertension reports new difficulty achieving erections that began several weeks after his medication regimen was adjusted. He currently takes metformin, atorvastatin, lisinopril, aspirin, and spironolactone. Which of the following medications is most likely contributing to his sexual dysfunction?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Aspirin

choices.label: B
choices.text: Atorvastatin

choices.label: C
choices.text: Lisinopril

choices.label: D
choices.text: Metformin

choices.label: E
choices.text: Spironolactone

explanation.summary: Spironolactone is among the medications recognized as common causes of sexual dysfunction.
explanation.whyCorrect: Medication review is an essential part of evaluating sexual dysfunction. Recognized medication contributors include antihistamines/H2 blockers, benzodiazepines, beta adrenergic agents, hormone replacement, opioids, spironolactone, SSRIs, and TCAs. Of this patient's medications, spironolactone is the one on that list.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Aspirin is not among the medications recognized as causing sexual dysfunction.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Atorvastatin is not among the listed medication causes of sexual dysfunction.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Lisinopril is not on the list of common medication contributors to sexual dysfunction.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Metformin is not among the medication classes identified as common causes of sexual dysfunction.

questions.stem: A 29-year-old woman reports 4 months of absent interest in sexual activity, no erotic thoughts or fantasies, and no arousal in response to cues she previously found stimulating. She is significantly distressed. Which of the following additional features is required before female sexual interest/arousal disorder can be diagnosed?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A desire level lower than that of her partner

choices.label: B
choices.text: Absence of all six diagnostic indicators

choices.label: C
choices.text: Failure of an adequate trial of flibanserin

choices.label: D
choices.text: Onset of the symptoms after menopause

choices.label: E
choices.text: Persistence of the symptoms for at least 6 months

explanation.summary: FSIAD requires absence or reduction of at least 3 of 6 indicators for at least 6 months with clinically significant distress.
explanation.whyCorrect: FSIAD is defined as absence or reduction of at least 3 of the 6 indicators for at least 6 months, causing clinically significant distress. This patient already has 3 absent indicators (interest in sexual activity, erotic thoughts/fantasies, arousal to cues) and distress, but her symptoms have lasted only 4 months, so the 6-month duration criterion is the missing requirement.

whyWrongByChoice.A: A desire discrepancy with a partner is explicitly insufficient for the diagnosis and is not a criterion.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Only 3 or more of the 6 indicators need to be absent or reduced, not all six.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Diagnosis does not depend on any medication trial; flibanserin is a treatment option, not a diagnostic requirement.
whyWrongByChoice.D: FSIAD is not restricted to postmenopausal onset; prevalence is 3-20% and varies by age.

questions.stem: A 45-year-old woman with female sexual interest/arousal disorder has had an inadequate response to CBT and couples therapy. Her physician prescribes a daily bedtime medication whose exact mechanism is unknown but is thought to alter central serotonergic signaling, reducing inhibitory input on sexual desire pathways. Which of the following medications was prescribed?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Amitriptyline

choices.label: B
choices.text: Bremelanotide

choices.label: C
choices.text: Dapoxetine

choices.label: D
choices.text: Flibanserin

choices.label: E
choices.text: Sildenafil

explanation.summary: Flibanserin is an FSIAD medication thought to alter central serotonergic signaling, reducing inhibitory input on sexual desire pathways.
explanation.whyCorrect: Flibanserin is a medication option for FSIAD after psychological interventions. Its exact mechanism is not known, but it is thought to alter central serotonergic signaling, which is believed to reduce inhibitory input on sexual desire pathways.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Amitriptyline is a tricyclic antidepressant used in GPPPD for chronic neuropathic pain via descending pain inhibition, not for FSIAD desire pathways.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Bremelanotide is an FSIAD option, but it is a melanocortin receptor agonist that acts centrally on desire and arousal pathways, not a serotonergic modulator.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Dapoxetine is a short-acting SSRI used on demand for premature ejaculation; it increases serotonin-mediated inhibition of ejaculation rather than reducing inhibition of desire.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Sildenafil is a PDE5 inhibitor that preserves cGMP to enhance genital blood flow; it is not a centrally acting serotonergic drug for desire.

questions.stem: A 41-year-old woman treated with an SSRI for major depressive disorder develops markedly reduced sexual desire and arousal that she attributes to the antidepressant. Her physician considers adding a medication whose mechanism can counter SSRI-related sexual dysfunction. Which of the following is the most appropriate choice?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Amitriptyline

choices.label: B
choices.text: Bremelanotide

choices.label: C
choices.text: Bupropion

choices.label: D
choices.text: Dapoxetine

choices.label: E
choices.text: Gabapentin

explanation.summary: Bupropion's norepinephrine-dopamine reuptake inhibition boosts catecholaminergic signaling without serotonergic sexual inhibition, countering SSRI-related sexual dysfunction.
explanation.whyCorrect: Bupropion inhibits norepinephrine and dopamine reuptake, increasing catecholaminergic signaling while avoiding serotonergic sexual inhibition. This mechanism may improve desire and arousal or counter SSRI-related sexual dysfunction, making it the fitting off-label choice here.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Amitriptyline inhibits norepinephrine and serotonin reuptake for chronic neuropathic pain; TCAs are themselves listed among medications that cause sexual dysfunction.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Bremelanotide is a melanocortin receptor agonist used for FSIAD; it is not the described strategy for countering SSRI-related dysfunction.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Dapoxetine is a short-acting SSRI for premature ejaculation; adding more serotonergic signaling would worsen, not counter, her problem.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Gabapentin dampens neuronal excitability via voltage-activated calcium channels for neuropathic pain in GPPPD; it does not restore desire or arousal.

questions.stem: A 38-year-old woman reports that for the past 8 months her orgasms have been markedly delayed and greatly reduced in intensity in nearly all of her sexual encounters, which distresses her significantly. She has normal desire, arousal, and lubrication and no pain. Which of the following is the most appropriate first-line management?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Daily sildenafil at bedtime

choices.label: B
choices.text: Daily SSRI therapy for the symptom

choices.label: C
choices.text: Pelvic floor physical therapy referral

choices.label: D
choices.text: Psychoeducation and behavioral therapy

choices.label: E
choices.text: Transdermal testosterone therapy

explanation.summary: Female orgasmic disorder is treated first with psychoeducation and behavioral therapy such as sexual skills training, CBT, and mindfulness-based therapy.
explanation.whyCorrect: She meets criteria for female orgasmic disorder: delay and reduced intensity of orgasm in at least 75% of sexual encounters for at least 6 months with significant distress. Psychoeducation and behavioral therapy, including sexual skills training, CBT, and mindfulness-based therapy, are first line.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Sildenafil is a medication option with limited data, most mechanistically plausible when orgasmic difficulty overlaps impaired genital arousal, which she does not have; it is not first line.
whyWrongByChoice.B: SSRIs increase serotonergic signaling that inhibits genital arousal reflexes and delays ejaculation and orgasm; they would worsen rather than treat her condition.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Pelvic floor physical therapy is the first-line treatment for genito-pelvic pain/penetration disorder; she has no pain or penetration difficulty.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Testosterone is an off-label medication option with limited data for orgasmic disorder, not initial management.

questions.stem: A 35-year-old woman with female orgasmic disorder continues to have absent orgasms despite ongoing sexual skills training and CBT. She also notes minimal genital engorgement and markedly reduced genital sensation of arousal during encounters. If a medication trial is pursued, which of the following options is most mechanistically appropriate for her presentation?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Dapoxetine

choices.label: B
choices.text: Flibanserin

choices.label: C
choices.text: Gabapentin

choices.label: D
choices.text: Sildenafil

choices.label: E
choices.text: Vaginal estrogen

explanation.summary: Sildenafil is most mechanistically plausible for orgasmic difficulty that overlaps with impaired genital arousal and engorgement.
explanation.whyCorrect: Sildenafil is a medication option for female orgasmic disorder: PDE5 inhibition preserves NO-mediated cGMP signaling, increasing genital smooth muscle relaxation and blood flow. This approach is most mechanistically plausible when orgasmic difficulty overlaps with impaired genital arousal and engorgement, which is exactly her pattern.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Dapoxetine is an on-demand SSRI for premature ejaculation; increasing serotonergic signaling inhibits arousal reflexes and would not help her reach orgasm.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Flibanserin is a medication option for FSIAD that modulates central serotonergic signaling to support desire; it is not the option aimed at deficient genital engorgement in orgasmic disorder.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Gabapentin dampens neuronal excitability for neuropathic pelvic pain in GPPPD; she has no pain component.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Vaginal estrogen restores vulvovaginal tissue in hypoestrogenic or atrophy-related dyspareunia; it is not the described option for orgasmic disorder with impaired engorgement.

questions.stem: A 27-year-old woman is diagnosed with genito-pelvic pain/penetration disorder after 8 months of pelvic pain with penetration, anticipatory anxiety, and pelvic floor tightening. When reviewing her medical history, the physician notes a comorbid condition that is a recognized risk factor for this disorder. Which of the following conditions is it most likely to be?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Asthma

choices.label: B
choices.text: Endometriosis

choices.label: C
choices.text: Hyperthyroidism

choices.label: D
choices.text: Iron deficiency anemia

choices.label: E
choices.text: Rheumatoid arthritis

explanation.summary: GPPPD risk factors include endometriosis, recurrent vaginitis or UTIs, IBS, bladder pain syndrome, mood and anxiety disorders, abuse history, and insecure attachment.
explanation.whyCorrect: Recognized risk factors for GPPPD include co-existing mood and anxiety disorders, a history of sexual or physical abuse, insecure attachment, recurrent vaginitis or UTIs, endometriosis, IBS, and bladder pain syndrome (interstitial cystitis). Of the conditions listed, endometriosis is the recognized risk factor.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Asthma is not associated with GPPPD among its recognized risk factors.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Hyperthyroidism is not among the listed risk factors for GPPPD.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Iron deficiency anemia is not a described risk factor for GPPPD.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Rheumatoid arthritis is not one of the conditions linked to GPPPD.

questions.stem: A 58-year-old postmenopausal woman has genito-pelvic pain/penetration disorder with burning pain on penetration. Examination shows thin, pale, dry vulvovaginal epithelium with loss of elasticity. She has begun pelvic floor physical therapy. Which of the following medications is most appropriate for the etiology of her pain?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Amitriptyline

choices.label: B
choices.text: An SNRI

choices.label: C
choices.text: Oral gabapentin

choices.label: D
choices.text: Topical lidocaine before intercourse

choices.label: E
choices.text: Topical vaginal estrogen

explanation.summary: GPPPD medications are chosen by etiology; vaginal estrogen is most useful for hypoestrogenic or atrophy-related dyspareunia.
explanation.whyCorrect: Medication options in GPPPD are dependent on etiology. Vaginal estrogen restores estrogen signaling in vulvovaginal tissue, improving epithelial thickness, lubrication, and tissue elasticity, and is most useful for hypoestrogenic or atrophy-related dyspareunia. This postmenopausal patient's thin, dry, inelastic epithelium points to exactly that etiology.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Amitriptyline strengthens descending pain inhibition for chronic neuropathic pain and would not correct the estrogen-deficient epithelium driving her symptoms.
whyWrongByChoice.B: SNRIs reduce centralized or neuropathic pelvic pain through descending inhibitory pathways, which is not the mechanism of her atrophy-related pain.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Gabapentin modulates voltage-activated calcium channels to dampen neuropathic pain signaling; it does not restore atrophic vulvovaginal tissue.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Local anesthetics block sodium channel-dependent conduction to blunt pain during penetration but leave the underlying epithelial atrophy untreated.

questions.stem: A 55-year-old man reports 1 year of progressive curvature of his penis with painful erections that now make intercourse very difficult. Examination reveals a firm plaque along the penile shaft. Which of the following treatments is most appropriate to address the underlying lesion?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Collagenase medication

choices.label: B
choices.text: Corporal aspiration

choices.label: C
choices.text: Daily sildenafil

choices.label: D
choices.text: Intracavernosal phenylephrine

choices.label: E
choices.text: On-demand dapoxetine

explanation.summary: Peyronie disease is caused by fibrous plaques around the corpora cavernosa and is treated with collagenase, ultrasound or radiation therapy, or surgery in severe cases.
explanation.whyCorrect: This is Peyronie disease, a distinct form of erectile dysfunction affecting males older than 40 that results from fibrous plaques of inflammation and scarring surrounding the corpora cavernosa. As plaques build, the penis bends, causing painful erections. Treatments include collagenase medication to break down the plaques, ultrasound or radiation therapy, and surgery for severe cases.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Corporal aspiration drains trapped blood in priapism and has no role in dissolving fibrous plaques.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Sildenafil enhances the NO-cGMP pathway for erectile dysfunction from impaired blood flow; it does not treat the plaque causing curvature and pain.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Intracavernosal phenylephrine opens veins in ischemic priapism, a sustained painful erection lasting more than 4 hours, not a fibrotic plaque disorder.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Dapoxetine is an on-demand SSRI for premature ejaculation and does not address penile curvature.

questions.stem: A 63-year-old man with erectile dysfunction has had inadequate improvement despite correctly timed, adequately dosed trials of both sildenafil and tadalafil with appropriate sexual stimulation. He wishes to pursue further treatment. Which of the following is the most appropriate next option?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Collagenase injection therapy

choices.label: B
choices.text: Corporal aspiration procedure

choices.label: C
choices.text: Daily dapoxetine treatment

choices.label: D
choices.text: Flibanserin taken at bedtime

choices.label: E
choices.text: Intracavernous injection therapy

explanation.summary: When first-line PDE5 inhibitors fail, second- and third-line options for erectile dysfunction include intracavernous injections, vacuum devices, and penile prosthesis.
explanation.whyCorrect: PDE5 inhibitors (sildenafil, tadalafil, vardenafil) are first line for erectile dysfunction. After an adequate failed trial, second- and third-line options include intracavernous injections, vacuum devices, and penile prosthesis. Of the choices offered, intracavernous injection therapy is the appropriate escalation.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Collagenase breaks down the fibrous plaques of Peyronie disease; he has no curvature or plaque.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Corporal aspiration treats ischemic priapism by draining trapped blood; it is not a therapy for erectile dysfunction.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Dapoxetine is a short-acting SSRI for premature ejaculation; SSRIs can cause rather than treat erectile problems.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Flibanserin is a medication option for female sexual interest/arousal disorder and has no role in male erectile dysfunction.

questions.stem: A 61-year-old man with newly diagnosed low-grade prostate cancer is deciding between radical prostatectomy and conservative management. He asks how surgery might affect his sexual function. Which of the following is the most accurate counseling statement?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Erectile dysfunction affects fewer than 5% of males after prostatectomy

choices.label: B
choices.text: Erectile dysfunction affects roughly 10% of males after prostatectomy

choices.label: C
choices.text: Erectile dysfunction after prostatectomy is nearly universal and permanent

choices.label: D
choices.text: Erectile dysfunction may affect as many as 50%-70% of males after prostatectomy

choices.label: E
choices.text: Erectile dysfunction occurs after prostatectomy only when radiation is also given

explanation.summary: ED may affect as many as 50%-70% of males undergoing prostatectomy, a key reason many choose conservative management of low-grade prostate cancer.
explanation.whyCorrect: Erectile dysfunction may affect as many as 50%-70% of males undergoing prostatectomy. This substantial risk is a reason that conservative management of low-grade prostate cancer is chosen by many patients, so it should be presented accurately during shared decision-making.

whyWrongByChoice.A: A figure under 5% drastically understates the 50%-70% risk described after prostatectomy.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Roughly 10% still greatly understates the described risk of postprostatectomy erectile dysfunction.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The risk is as many as 50%-70%, not nearly 100%, and treatments such as PDE5 inhibitors, injections, vacuum devices, and prosthesis remain available.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The 50%-70% figure applies to prostatectomy itself; it is not contingent on added radiation therapy.

questions.stem: A 48-year-old female reports 8 months of menstrual cycles that have become progressively lighter and farther apart, along with new nighttime episodes of sudden warmth, flushing, and sweating that wake her from sleep. Her last menstrual period was 6 weeks ago. A urine pregnancy test is negative. Which of the following best characterizes her current reproductive state?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Menopause, because vasomotor symptoms have begun

choices.label: B
choices.text: Perimenopause, the transition preceding the final menstrual period

choices.label: C
choices.text: Postmenopause, because her cycles are lighter than baseline

choices.label: D
choices.text: Premature ovarian insufficiency, because she is younger than 51

choices.label: E
choices.text: Secondary amenorrhea, because her cycle length has increased

explanation.summary: Irregular, spaced-out cycles with new vasomotor symptoms in the 40s define perimenopause; menopause requires 12 consecutive months of amenorrhea.
explanation.whyCorrect: Perimenopause is the interval of years before the final menstrual period marked by fluctuating hormone levels, irregular cycles, and the onset of vasomotor symptoms, typically beginning in the 40s or 50s and lasting 2-8 years. Because this patient is still menstruating, she has not met the diagnostic criterion for menopause.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Menopause is diagnosed retrospectively after 12 consecutive months of amenorrhea, not by the onset of hot flashes; she menstruated 6 weeks ago.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Postmenopause refers to the years after menopause has occurred; she has not yet reached menopause.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Onset of the menopausal transition in the late 40s is typical, not premature; the average age of menopause is 51, with 90% between 45 and 56.
whyWrongByChoice.E: She continues to menstruate, so she does not have amenorrhea; her irregular cycles reflect the normal menopausal transition.

questions.stem: A 52-year-old female with 14 months of amenorrhea undergoes laboratory testing. Her physician notes that one hormonal change is considered the primary indicator of menopause. An increase in which of the following, driven by loss of a specific ovarian follicular product, best fits this description?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Estrone, due to peripheral aromatization of androgens

choices.label: B
choices.text: FSH, due to decreased inhibin B production

choices.label: C
choices.text: GnRH, due to loss of progesterone negative feedback

choices.label: D
choices.text: LH, due to loss of estrogen negative feedback

choices.label: E
choices.text: Prolactin, due to loss of dopaminergic inhibition

explanation.summary: The primary hormonal change indicating menopause is a marked rise in FSH, driven by decreased inhibin B production from ovarian follicles.
explanation.whyCorrect: With loss of ovarian follicular activity, follicles no longer produce inhibin B, releasing FSH from its selective negative feedback. FSH therefore rises markedly and is the primary hormonal indicator of menopause, alongside decreased estrogen and progesterone and increased LH and GnRH.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Ovarian estrogen production falls in menopause; a rise in estrogen is not the hormonal marker of menopause.
whyWrongByChoice.C: GnRH rises, but it is not singled out as the primary indicator, and inhibin B loss specifically drives FSH.
whyWrongByChoice.D: LH does rise in menopause, but the lecture identifies the FSH increase, driven by lost inhibin B, as the primary indicator.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Prolactin is not part of the hormonal profile of menopause described in this lecture.

questions.stem: A 60-year-old female who reached menopause at age 51 presents with two episodes of light vaginal spotting over the past month. She takes no hormone therapy. Which of the following is the most likely cause of her bleeding?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Cervical infection

choices.label: B
choices.text: Endometrial atrophy

choices.label: C
choices.text: Endometrial cancer

choices.label: D
choices.text: Endometrial polyp

choices.label: E
choices.text: Resumption of ovulation

explanation.summary: Endometrial atrophy is the most common cause of postmenopausal bleeding.
explanation.whyCorrect: Postmenopausal bleeding is most commonly caused by endometrial atrophy; other causes include endometrial polyps and hormone replacement therapy. Only approximately 10% of postmenopausal bleeding is caused by endometrial cancer.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Infection is not among the leading causes of postmenopausal bleeding taught here; atrophy remains most likely.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Endometrial cancer accounts for only about 10% of postmenopausal bleeding; it must be considered but is not the most likely cause.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Endometrial polyps cause postmenopausal bleeding but are less common than atrophy as the etiology.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Menopause is a permanent cessation of menses from loss of ovarian follicular activity; ovulation does not resume 9 years later.

questions.stem: A 53-year-old female with an intact uterus has severe hot flashes and night sweats that have not improved with lifestyle changes. She and her physician decide to start systemic estrogen therapy. Adding a progestogen to her regimen is necessary primarily to reduce the risk of which of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Deep vein thrombosis and pulmonary embolism

choices.label: B
choices.text: Endometrial hyperplasia and cancer

choices.label: C
choices.text: Invasive breast cancer and recurrence

choices.label: D
choices.text: Ischemic stroke and coronary events

choices.label: E
choices.text: Recurrent urinary tract infection

explanation.summary: In a female with an intact uterus, a progestogen must accompany systemic estrogen to prevent endometrial hyperplasia and cancer from unopposed estrogen.
explanation.whyCorrect: Unopposed systemic estrogen stimulates the endometrium and can cause endometrial hyperplasia and cancer. Combined estrogen-progestogen therapy is therefore required for females with an intact uterus, whereas females who have had a hysterectomy can use estrogen-only therapy.

whyWrongByChoice.A: VTE is a risk of hormone therapy itself, mitigated by transdermal rather than oral routes, not by adding a progestogen.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Breast cancer risk was increased in the WHI combined estrogen-progestogen arm; progestogen does not protect against it.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Stroke is a risk of hormone therapy (seen even in the estrogen-only WHI arm); progestogen does not prevent it.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Estrogen therapy decreases UTI risk; UTI prevention is not the purpose of the progestogen.

questions.stem: A 54-year-old female with moderate vasomotor symptoms is choosing between oral and transdermal estradiol. Her physician explains that the transdermal route carries lower risks of venous thromboembolism and stroke. Which of the following best explains this difference?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Transdermal estrogen acts as a receptor antagonist in the liver

choices.label: B
choices.text: Transdermal estrogen bypasses first-pass hepatic metabolism

choices.label: C
choices.text: Transdermal estrogen is absorbed only by urogenital tissues

choices.label: D
choices.text: Transdermal estrogen is converted to progesterone in the skin

choices.label: E
choices.text: Transdermal estrogen raises sex hormone-binding globulin levels

explanation.summary: Transdermal estrogens avoid first-pass hepatic metabolism, so they do not increase hepatic production of clotting factors the way oral estrogens do.
explanation.whyCorrect: Oral estrogens undergo first-pass hepatic metabolism, which increases production of clotting factors, inflammatory markers, and sex hormone-binding globulin. Transdermal patches, gels, and sprays bypass this first pass, producing more stable hormone levels and lower risks of venous thromboembolism and stroke.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Transdermal estrogen is not a hepatic receptor antagonist; tissue-selective agonist/antagonist activity describes SERMs like ospemifene.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Delivery limited to urogenital tissue describes low-dose vaginal estrogen, not systemic transdermal therapy, which treats vasomotor symptoms.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Estrogen is not converted to progesterone in the skin; this is not a described mechanism.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Raising SHBG is an effect of oral estrogen's first-pass metabolism, the very effect transdermal dosing avoids.

questions.stem: A 58-year-old female with an intact uterus reports vaginal dryness, pain with intercourse, and two urinary tract infections in the past year. She denies hot flashes or night sweats. Which of the following is the most appropriate therapy?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Low-dose local estrogen therapy without a progestogen

choices.label: B
choices.text: Oral conjugated equine estrogens with a progestogen

choices.label: C
choices.text: Oral gabapentin at bedtime

choices.label: D
choices.text: Oral paroxetine at bedtime

choices.label: E
choices.text: Transdermal estradiol patch with a progestogen

explanation.summary: Isolated genitourinary symptoms are best treated with low-dose vaginal estrogen, which needs no progestogen even with an intact uterus.
explanation.whyCorrect: For females with primarily genitourinary symptoms and no significant vasomotor symptoms, low-dose vaginal estrogen is preferred. Creams, tablets, and rings deliver estrogen directly to urogenital tissue with minimal systemic absorption, treating dryness, dyspareunia, and recurrent UTIs, and the minimal endometrial exposure means no concurrent progestogen is required.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Systemic oral estrogen adds thromboembolic and other systemic risks she does not need, since she has no vasomotor symptoms.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Gabapentin helps hot flashes and night sweats, not vaginal dryness, dyspareunia, or recurrent UTIs.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Paroxetine targets vasomotor symptoms, which she does not have, and does not treat atrophic genitourinary changes.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Systemic transdermal therapy is likewise unnecessary for purely genitourinary symptoms that local therapy treats effectively.

questions.stem: A 51-year-old female with a history of estrogen receptor-positive breast cancer, now in remission, has frequent daytime hot flashes. She asks about medication options. Which of the following is FDA-approved specifically for menopausal hot flashes?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Citalopram

choices.label: B
choices.text: Desvenlafaxine

choices.label: C
choices.text: Escitalopram

choices.label: D
choices.text: Paroxetine

choices.label: E
choices.text: Venlafaxine

explanation.summary: Paroxetine is the SSRI that is FDA-approved for menopausal hot flashes; hormone therapy is contraindicated with current or hormone-sensitive cancer history.
explanation.whyCorrect: Hormone-sensitive breast cancer is a contraindication to hormone replacement therapy, so a non-hormonal agent is appropriate. Among SSRIs/SNRIs used for vasomotor symptoms, paroxetine is specifically FDA-approved for menopausal hot flashes; the class reduces hot flash frequency by roughly 40-60%.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Citalopram has shown benefit in trials but is not FDA-approved for hot flashes.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Desvenlafaxine has trial evidence of benefit but is not the FDA-approved agent.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Escitalopram has trial evidence of benefit but lacks FDA approval for hot flashes.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Venlafaxine has shown benefit in clinical trials but is not FDA-approved for this indication.

questions.stem: A 55-year-old female has drenching night sweats that repeatedly wake her, and she cannot fall back asleep afterward. She declines hormone therapy. Which non-hormonal medication, taken at bedtime, is particularly well suited to her presentation?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Gabapentin, via calcium channel modulation and sedation

choices.label: B
choices.text: Ospemifene, via estrogen agonism in vaginal tissue

choices.label: C
choices.text: Oxybutynin, via inhibition of sweat gland activity

choices.label: D
choices.text: Paroxetine, via serotonin reuptake inhibition

choices.label: E
choices.text: Venlafaxine, via norepinephrine reuptake inhibition

explanation.summary: Gabapentin's sedating properties make it especially useful for night sweats with sleep disturbance when dosed at bedtime.
explanation.whyCorrect: Gabapentin is an anticonvulsant that modulates calcium channels and affects thermoregulation, reducing hot flashes by approximately 50%. Its sedating effect, ordinarily a side effect, becomes an advantage for females whose vasomotor symptoms are concentrated at night and disrupt sleep.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Ospemifene treats dyspareunia from vulvovaginal atrophy; it has no role in vasomotor symptoms or sleep.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Oxybutynin has efficacy for hot flashes but offers no sleep benefit, and anticholinergic effects limit its use in older females.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Paroxetine helps vasomotor symptoms but is not highlighted for bedtime dosing to aid sleep the way gabapentin is.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Venlafaxine reduces hot flashes but is not the sedating bedtime option suited to nighttime symptoms.

questions.stem: A 62-year-old female with painful intercourse due to vulvovaginal atrophy prefers an oral medication over vaginal preparations. Her physician prescribes ospemifene. Which of the following best describes this drug's mechanism of action?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Anticholinergic inhibitor of glandular secretion in the vagina and vulva

choices.label: B
choices.text: Aromatase inhibitor that raises local estradiol concentrations in the vagina

choices.label: C
choices.text: Estrogen receptor agonist in vaginal tissue, neutral or antagonist elsewhere

choices.label: D
choices.text: Estrogen receptor antagonist in vaginal tissue, agonist in bone and the uterus

choices.label: E
choices.text: Progesterone receptor agonist acting on the endometrium and myometrium

explanation.summary: Ospemifene is an oral SERM that acts as an estrogen agonist in vaginal tissue while remaining neutral or antagonist in other tissues.
explanation.whyCorrect: Ospemifene is an oral selective estrogen receptor modulator approved for dyspareunia associated with vulvovaginal atrophy. Its tissue selectivity, agonist activity in vaginal tissue with neutral or antagonist effects elsewhere, allows it to treat atrophic symptoms without generalized estrogenic stimulation.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Anticholinergic inhibition of glands describes oxybutynin's effect on sweat glands, not ospemifene.
whyWrongByChoice.B: It does not inhibit aromatase; aromatase inhibition would lower, not exploit, estrogenic signaling.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Its agonist activity is in vaginal tissue; it is not a vaginal antagonist.
whyWrongByChoice.E: It modulates estrogen receptors, not progesterone receptors, and is not endometrium-targeted therapy.

questions.stem: A 63-year-old female, 12 years postmenopausal, is found to have low bone mineral density on screening. Which of the following cellular changes best explains the accelerated bone loss that follows menopause?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Decreased osteoclast activity with increased osteoblast activity

choices.label: B
choices.text: Decreased osteocyte density with increased mineralization

choices.label: C
choices.text: Increased chondrocyte proliferation at the growth plate

choices.label: D
choices.text: Increased osteoblast activity with normal osteoclast activity

choices.label: E
choices.text: Increased osteoclast activity with decreased osteoblast activity

explanation.summary: Estrogen loss after menopause increases osteoclast activity and decreases osteoblast activity, producing osteoporosis.
explanation.whyCorrect: Declining estrogen removes its restraint on bone resorption: osteoclast activity increases while osteoblast activity decreases, tipping remodeling toward net bone loss. This is why postmenopausal females are at elevated risk of osteoporosis, and why HRT produces significant fracture reduction.

whyWrongByChoice.A: This pattern would build bone rather than lose it, the opposite of postmenopausal physiology.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Changes in mineralization density are not the mechanism taught; the imbalance is between osteoclasts and osteoblasts.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Growth plates are closed in adults; chondrocyte proliferation is irrelevant to postmenopausal bone loss.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Osteoblast activity falls, not rises, after estrogen loss, and osteoclast activity is increased.

questions.stem: A 58-year-old male reports several years of slowly worsening fatigue, reduced libido, and fewer morning erections. His physician explains how age-related testosterone decline differs from menopause. Which of the following statements best captures that difference?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Testosterone ceases abruptly once Leydig cell activity is lost at a set age

choices.label: B
choices.text: Testosterone decline arises only from failure of hypothalamic GnRH output

choices.label: C
choices.text: Testosterone decline is diagnosed after 12 months of absent morning erections

choices.label: D
choices.text: Testosterone decline spares free testosterone because SHBG falls with age

choices.label: E
choices.text: Testosterone declines gradually at about 1% per year without defined stages

explanation.summary: Unlike menopause, andropause is a gradual, stage-less decline in testosterone of roughly 1% per year beginning around age 40.
explanation.whyCorrect: Beginning around age 40, testosterone falls about 1% per year, with the decline more pronounced in free testosterone because of alterations in sex hormone-binding globulin. In contrast to menopause, andropause has a gradual onset and slow progression without defined stages, and it results from both central (hypothalamic-pituitary) and peripheral (Leydig cell responsiveness) mechanisms.

whyWrongByChoice.A: There is no abrupt cessation at a set age; abrupt loss of gonadal hormone output is the pattern of menopause, not andropause.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The decline is both central (decreased hypothalamic-pituitary function) and peripheral (reduced Leydig cell responsiveness), not purely central.
whyWrongByChoice.C: No 12-month diagnostic criterion exists for andropause; that retrospective rule defines menopause.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Free testosterone falls more, not less, because of SHBG alterations with age.

questions.stem: A 61-year-old male with symptomatic hypogonadism confirmed by low serum testosterone begins intramuscular testosterone replacement therapy. Three months later his testosterone level is 950 ng/dL. Continuing this dose places him at increased risk for which of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Cardiovascular complications and suppressed spermatogenesis

choices.label: B
choices.text: Endometrial hyperplasia from unopposed hormone exposure

choices.label: C
choices.text: Hot flashes from hypothalamic thermoregulatory dysfunction

choices.label: D
choices.text: Osteoporosis and progressive loss of muscle mass

choices.label: E
choices.text: Worsening erectile dysfunction and reduced libido

explanation.summary: Testosterone replacement should target the physiologic range of 400-700 ng/dL; supratherapeutic levels raise the risk of cardiovascular complications, BPH, and suppressed spermatogenesis.
explanation.whyCorrect: The goal of testosterone replacement therapy is a level within the physiologic range of 400-700 ng/dL with symptom improvement. At 950 ng/dL this patient is supratherapeutic, which may increase the risk of cardiovascular complications, benign prostatic hyperplasia, and suppression of spermatogenesis.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Endometrial hyperplasia is a risk of unopposed estrogen in females with a uterus, not of testosterone therapy in males.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Hot flashes from estrogen withdrawal are a menopausal phenomenon, not a described risk of excess testosterone.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Bone and muscle loss are consequences of low testosterone, not of supratherapeutic replacement.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Erectile dysfunction and low libido are symptoms of hypogonadism that therapy aims to improve, not risks of excess dosing.

questions.stem: A 46-year-old female has had no menstrual bleeding for 12 consecutive months and reports hot flashes and vaginal dryness. Pregnancy and other causes of amenorrhea have been excluded. She asks whether reaching menopause at her age is unusual. Which of the following best describes the age distribution of menopause in the United States?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Average age 45 years, with 90% between 40 and 50 years

choices.label: B
choices.text: Average age 48 years, with 90% between 42 and 53 years

choices.label: C
choices.text: Average age 51 years, with 90% between 45 and 56 years

choices.label: D
choices.text: Average age 54 years, with 90% between 48 and 60 years

choices.label: E
choices.text: Average age 57 years, with 90% between 51 and 63 years

explanation.summary: The average age of menopause in the United States is 51, with 90% of females reaching it between ages 45 and 56.
explanation.whyCorrect: Menopause occurs at an average age of 51 in the United States, and 90% of females experience it between 45 and 56 years. At 46 this patient is within the usual range, simply toward its earlier end, so no additional workup for early ovarian failure is implied by her age alone.

whyWrongByChoice.A: An average of 45 is several years earlier than the figure taught, and would misclassify most typical menopause as late.
whyWrongByChoice.B: An average of 48 understates the typical age and narrows the range incorrectly.
whyWrongByChoice.D: An average of 54 is later than taught and would wrongly label this patient's menopause as premature.
whyWrongByChoice.E: An average of 57 is far later than the taught figure; most females are already postmenopausal by that age.

questions.stem: A 50-year-old female has had no menstrual bleeding for 13 months. During that interval she was hospitalized twice for severe illness and was treated with a medication known to suppress menstruation. She reports no hot flashes, night sweats, or vaginal dryness. Which of the following is most appropriate before attributing her amenorrhea to menopause?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Confirm that no other pathologic or physiologic cause explains the amenorrhea

choices.label: B
choices.text: Demonstrate an estradiol level above the premenopausal reference range

choices.label: C
choices.text: Document at least 24 consecutive months of amenorrhea

choices.label: D
choices.text: Establish that vasomotor symptoms preceded the final menstrual period

choices.label: E
choices.text: Verify that her mother reached menopause at a comparable age

explanation.summary: Menopause is a diagnosis of exclusion made retrospectively: 12 months of amenorrhea with no other identifiable pathologic or physiologic cause.
explanation.whyCorrect: Menopause is clinically defined as permanent cessation of menstruation from loss of ovarian follicular activity, diagnosed retrospectively after 12 consecutive months of amenorrhea for which no other obvious pathologic or physiologic cause can be determined. That qualifier exists precisely to separate menopause from temporary cessation of menses caused by pregnancy, lactation, severe illness, or certain medications, all of which are in play here.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Estrogen production falls in menopause, so a high estradiol level would argue against it rather than confirm it.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The diagnostic interval is 12 consecutive months, not 24; lengthening it does not resolve the competing causes present in this case.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Vasomotor symptoms vary widely and are not required for the diagnosis; this patient has none yet still may be menopausal.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Family history is not part of the clinical definition of menopause and would not exclude illness or medication as the cause.

questions.stem: A 44-year-old female has had unpredictable, increasingly spaced menstrual cycles and intermittent hot flashes for the past 10 months. She asks how long this phase typically lasts before menstruation stops altogether. Which of the following is the best estimate?

choices.label: A
choices.text: 1 to 3 months

choices.label: B
choices.text: 2 to 8 years

choices.label: C
choices.text: 6 to 12 months

choices.label: D
choices.text: 10 to 15 years

choices.label: E
choices.text: 20 to 25 years

explanation.summary: Perimenopause usually begins in the 40s or 50s and can last 2-8 years before menstruation ceases.
explanation.whyCorrect: Perimenopause, the menopausal transition, is the interval of years preceding the final menstrual period during which hormone levels fluctuate, cycles become irregular, and vasomotor symptoms begin. It typically starts in the 40s or 50s and can last 2-8 years before menstruation stops.

whyWrongByChoice.A: A few months is far shorter than the transition, which spans years of fluctuating hormones and irregular cycles.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Less than a year understates the transition; 12 months of amenorrhea is the criterion for menopause itself, not the length of perimenopause.
whyWrongByChoice.D: A decade or more overstates the taught duration of the transition.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Two decades far exceeds the taught duration; that interval would approach the postmenopausal years instead.

questions.stem: A 52-year-old female whose final menstrual period was 14 months ago asks how much of her life she can expect to spend in the postmenopausal state, given her risks of osteoporosis and cardiovascular disease. Approximately what proportion is correct?

explanation.summary: Females spend approximately 40% of their lives postmenopausal, which is why long-term postmenopausal risks matter so much.
explanation.whyCorrect: Postmenopause refers to the years following menopause, during which symptoms may persist; females spend approximately 40% of their life in this state. Over that span they carry a higher risk of osteoporosis, genitourinary complications, cardiovascular disease, and metabolic disorders, which is why long-term risk reduction is part of management.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Ten percent would be only about 8 years of life after menopause, far less than the taught figure.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Twenty-five percent underestimates the postmenopausal share of the lifespan.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Sixty percent would place menopause in the early 30s for an average lifespan, which conflicts with an average menopausal age of 51.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Seventy-five percent is far too high and is inconsistent with the average age of menopause.

questions.stem: A 53-year-old female, 2 years past her final menstrual period, describes abrupt episodes of intense heat that begin in her head, neck, and chest and are followed by flushing and profuse sweating, each lasting a few minutes. Which of the following best explains these episodes?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Hypothalamic thermoregulatory dysfunction due to estrogen withdrawal

choices.label: B
choices.text: Increased osteoclastic activity with decreased osteoblast function

choices.label: C
choices.text: Loss of estrogen's vasodilatory and anti-inflammatory vascular effects

choices.label: D
choices.text: Rising inhibin B output from remaining ovarian follicles

choices.label: E
choices.text: Urethral epithelial thinning with decreased pelvic floor tone

explanation.summary: Hot flashes arise from hypothalamic thermoregulatory dysfunction caused by estrogen withdrawal.
explanation.whyCorrect: A hot flash is a sudden feeling of heat usually in the head, neck, and chest, though it may involve the whole body, and it results from dysfunction of hypothalamic thermoregulation once estrogen is withdrawn. The same mechanism produces night sweats, which is why vasomotor symptoms respond so well to estrogen replacement.

whyWrongByChoice.B: That imbalance drives accelerated bone loss and osteoporosis, not episodic heat and flushing.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Loss of estrogen's vasodilatory and anti-inflammatory effects underlies the rise in cardiovascular risk, not the thermoregulatory episodes.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Inhibin B production falls with loss of follicular activity; that fall raises FSH and does not cause hot flashes.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Urethral thinning and reduced pelvic floor tone explain urinary symptoms such as incontinence.

questions.stem: A 59-year-old female, 7 years past her final menstrual period, reports involuntary leakage of urine when she coughs, laughs, or lifts objects. She has no dysuria and urine culture is negative. Which of the following best explains her symptom?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Hypothalamic thermoregulatory dysfunction due to estrogen withdrawal

choices.label: B
choices.text: Increased central adiposity with rising insulin resistance

choices.label: C
choices.text: Increased osteoclastic activity with decreased osteoblast function

choices.label: D
choices.text: Thinning of the urethral epithelium with decreased pelvic floor tone

choices.label: E
choices.text: Unopposed estrogen stimulation of the endometrial lining

explanation.summary: Postmenopausal urinary incontinence reflects estrogen-dependent urethral epithelial thinning together with decreased pelvic floor tone.
explanation.whyCorrect: Urinary incontinence is among the common symptoms of menopause, and its physiologic basis is thinning of the urethral epithelium plus decreased pelvic floor tone after estrogen loss. These tissues are estrogen-responsive, which is why local vaginal estrogen improves urogenital symptoms including recurrent urinary tract infections.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Thermoregulatory dysfunction produces hot flashes and night sweats, not stress leakage of urine.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Central adiposity and insulin resistance contribute to cardiovascular and metabolic risk, not to urethral support.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The osteoclast-osteoblast imbalance causes accelerated bone loss and osteoporosis.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Unopposed estrogen stimulation drives endometrial hyperplasia and bleeding; estrogen here is deficient, not excessive.

questions.stem: A 57-year-old postmenopausal female has had three episodes of vaginitis and two urinary tract infections over 18 months. Pelvic examination shows pale vaginal walls with loss of rugae, and vaginal pH is elevated. Which of the following best explains her increased susceptibility to these infections?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Estrogen deficiency raising vaginal pH and shifting the urogenital microbiome

choices.label: B
choices.text: Increased central adiposity with worsening insulin resistance and dyslipidemia

choices.label: C
choices.text: Loss of estrogen's vasodilatory and anti-inflammatory effects on blood vessels

choices.label: D
choices.text: Rising LH and GnRH pulses driving endometrial glandular proliferation

choices.label: E
choices.text: Unopposed estrogen stimulation of atrophic vaginal and bladder tissue

explanation.summary: Genitourinary syndrome of menopause results from estrogen loss that raises vaginal pH, thins tissue, and alters the urogenital microbiome, increasing infection risk.
explanation.whyCorrect: In genitourinary syndrome of menopause, declining estrogen raises vaginal pH, reduces vaginal rugae, tissue elasticity, and lubrication, and changes the urogenital microbiome. Those changes increase the risk of vaginitis, urinary tract infection, dyspareunia, pruritus, and burning, exactly the pattern seen on this patient's exam.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Central adiposity and insulin resistance are metabolic consequences of menopause and do not explain the elevated vaginal pH and loss of rugae.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Loss of estrogen's vascular effects contributes to cardiovascular risk, not to recurrent urogenital infection.
whyWrongByChoice.D: LH and GnRH do rise in menopause, but the endometrium atrophies rather than proliferates, and gonadotropins do not drive these infections.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Her tissues show estrogen deficiency, not unopposed estrogen stimulation, which instead causes endometrial hyperplasia.

questions.stem: A 55-year-old female, 4 years past her final menstrual period, has no chronic illnesses and takes no medications. Her physician counsels her that menopause itself alters her cardiovascular risk profile. Which of the following changes is most expected?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Decreased LDL cholesterol with decreased insulin resistance

choices.label: B
choices.text: Decreased LDL cholesterol with increased HDL cholesterol

choices.label: C
choices.text: Increased HDL cholesterol with decreased central adiposity

choices.label: D
choices.text: Increased LDL cholesterol with decreased HDL cholesterol

choices.label: E
choices.text: Unchanged cholesterol levels with decreased insulin resistance

explanation.summary: Menopause shifts lipids unfavorably, raising LDL and lowering HDL, one component of the increased cardiovascular risk after estrogen loss.
explanation.whyCorrect: Increased cardiovascular disease risk after menopause reflects changes in lipid metabolism with increased LDL and decreased HDL, changes in glucose metabolism with increased insulin resistance, and changes in body fat distribution with increased central adiposity. Loss of estrogen's vasodilatory and anti-inflammatory effects compounds this risk.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Insulin resistance increases rather than decreases after menopause, and LDL rises rather than falls.
whyWrongByChoice.B: This is the favorable lipid pattern, the opposite of what follows estrogen loss.
whyWrongByChoice.C: HDL falls and central adiposity increases after menopause, so both halves of this option are reversed.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Lipids do change with menopause, and insulin resistance rises rather than improves.

questions.stem: A 54-year-old postmenopausal female has gained 12 pounds over 2 years despite no change in her diet or activity level, and her waist circumference has increased. Which of the following best accounts for these changes?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Excess ovarian estrogen promoting peripheral fat deposition

choices.label: B
choices.text: Increased HDL cholesterol with improved insulin sensitivity

choices.label: C
choices.text: Increased osteoblast activity with expansion of bone mass

choices.label: D
choices.text: Rising inhibin B levels stimulating appetite

choices.label: E
choices.text: Slowed metabolism with redistribution of body fat centrally

explanation.summary: Menopausal weight gain is attributed to a slowed metabolism, accompanied by a shift toward central fat distribution.
explanation.whyCorrect: Weight gain due to slowed metabolism is among the common symptoms of menopause. In parallel, altered body fat distribution with increased central adiposity is one of the changes that raises postmenopausal cardiovascular and metabolic risk, matching this patient's rising waist circumference.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Ovarian estrogen production declines in menopause; estrogen excess is not the explanation.
whyWrongByChoice.B: HDL decreases and insulin resistance increases after menopause, the reverse of this option.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Osteoblast activity decreases after menopause, and bone mass falls rather than expands; this would not cause weight gain.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Inhibin B production falls with loss of follicular activity, and it is not described as an appetite regulator.

questions.stem: A 50-year-old female in the menopausal transition reports irritability, low mood, and difficulty concentrating over several months. Night sweats wake her repeatedly during the night and is also the primary caregiver for an ill parent. Which of the following best describes the basis of her mood symptoms?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Decreased vaginal epithelial thickness, lubrication, and elasticity

choices.label: B
choices.text: Hormonal fluctuation, sleep disruption, and psychosocial factors together

choices.label: C
choices.text: Hypothalamic thermoregulatory dysfunction from estrogen withdrawal

choices.label: D
choices.text: Increased osteoclastic activity with decreased osteoblast function

choices.label: E
choices.text: Rising inhibin B from recruitment of new ovarian follicles

explanation.summary: Mood changes in the menopausal transition are multifactorial: fluctuating hormones, disrupted sleep, and psychosocial stressors.
explanation.whyCorrect: Mood changes are a common menopausal symptom, and their basis is hormonal fluctuation compounded by sleep disruption and psychosocial factors. Her night sweats fragment sleep and her caregiving burden adds psychosocial stress, so management is individualized rather than aimed at a single cause.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Vaginal atrophy explains dryness and dyspareunia, not irritability and poor concentration.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Thermoregulatory dysfunction explains her hot flashes and night sweats, which are contributors to, not the mechanism of, her mood symptoms.
whyWrongByChoice.D: That imbalance causes accelerated bone loss and has no role in mood.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Inhibin B falls during the transition as follicles are depleted; new follicles are not being recruited.

questions.stem: A 52-year-old female with frequent disabling hot flashes and no contraindications to hormone therapy asks how much more benefit she would get from hormone therapy than from an SSRI or SNRI. Which of the following comparisons is accurate?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Hormone therapy reduces hot flashes 30%; SSRIs and SNRIs about 30%

choices.label: B
choices.text: Hormone therapy reduces hot flashes 40-60%; SSRIs and SNRIs 75-80%

choices.label: C
choices.text: Hormone therapy reduces hot flashes 50%; SSRIs and SNRIs about 10%

choices.label: D
choices.text: Hormone therapy reduces hot flashes 75-80%; SSRIs and SNRIs 40-60%

choices.label: E
choices.text: Hormone therapy reduces hot flashes 90-95%; SSRIs and SNRIs 75-80%

explanation.summary: Systemic hormone therapy cuts hot flash frequency and severity by 75-80%, while SSRIs and SNRIs achieve roughly 40-60%.
explanation.whyCorrect: Hormone replacement therapy remains the most effective treatment for vasomotor symptoms, reducing hot flash frequency and severity by 75-80% and outperforming placebo and non-hormonal alternatives. SSRIs and SNRIs are effective but less so, typically reducing hot flash frequency by 40-60%; gabapentin reduces them by about 50%.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Both figures understate efficacy, and hormone therapy is clearly superior rather than equivalent.
whyWrongByChoice.B: This reverses the two figures; the antidepressants are the less effective option, not the more effective one.
whyWrongByChoice.C: SSRIs and SNRIs do substantially better than 10%, and hormone therapy exceeds 50%.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Hormone therapy is not 90-95% effective, and this overstates SSRI and SNRI efficacy as well.

questions.stem: A 53-year-old female with an intact uterus and bothersome vasomotor symptoms is weighing systemic hormone therapy and asks what else it might do for her health. Besides relief of hot flashes, which of the following is an established benefit of this therapy?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Reduced risk of invasive breast cancer

choices.label: B
choices.text: Reduced risk of ischemic stroke

choices.label: C
choices.text: Reduced risk of postmenopausal bleeding

choices.label: D
choices.text: Reduced risk of venous thromboembolism

choices.label: E
choices.text: Significant reduction in fracture risk

explanation.summary: Hormone therapy's benefits include significant fracture reduction, fewer urinary tract infections, and lower diabetes and colorectal cancer risk; stroke, thromboembolism, breast cancer, and bleeding are its risks.
explanation.whyCorrect: Benefits of hormone replacement therapy include improvement in vasomotor symptoms, significant fracture reduction, decreased urinary tract infections, and decreased diabetes and colorectal cancer risk. The fracture benefit follows directly from restoring estrogen's restraint on bone resorption after menopause.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Breast cancer is a listed risk and was the finding that ended the combined estrogen-progestogen trial arm.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Stroke is a listed risk of hormone therapy, and it was the finding that ended the estrogen-only trial arm.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Postmenopausal bleeding is a listed risk of hormone therapy and one of its recognized causes.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Deep venous thrombosis is a listed risk, higher with oral than transdermal preparations.

questions.stem: A 54-year-old female with severe hot flashes asks about systemic hormone therapy. Her history includes a deep venous thrombosis after knee surgery 3 years ago, well-controlled hypothyroidism, osteopenia on screening, and a maternal aunt with colon cancer. Which element of her history is a contraindication to systemic hormone therapy?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Age older than 50 years

choices.label: B
choices.text: Family history of colon cancer

choices.label: C
choices.text: Osteopenia on screening

choices.label: D
choices.text: Prior deep venous thrombosis

choices.label: E
choices.text: Well-controlled hypothyroidism

explanation.summary: A history of DVT or stroke is a contraindication to hormone replacement therapy.
explanation.whyCorrect: Contraindications to hormone replacement therapy include current hormone-sensitive cancer such as breast or endometrial cancer, a history of deep venous thrombosis or stroke, significant coronary artery disease, and liver disease. Her prior DVT therefore rules out systemic therapy, and non-hormonal options should be used instead.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Being in her 50s places her within the window of opportunity rather than excluding her from treatment.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Hormone therapy is associated with decreased colorectal cancer risk; a family history of colon cancer is not a contraindication.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Low bone density is a reason to consider therapy, since hormone therapy produces significant fracture reduction.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Thyroid disease is not among the contraindications to hormone therapy.

questions.stem: In the Women's Health Initiative, postmenopausal females with an intact uterus received conjugated equine estrogens plus medroxyprogesterone acetate, while those with a prior hysterectomy received conjugated equine estrogens alone. Each arm was stopped early for a different safety signal. Which of the following correctly pairs the regimen with the finding that ended it?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Combined arm, deep venous thrombosis; estrogen-alone arm, endometrial cancer

choices.label: B
choices.text: Combined arm, endometrial cancer; estrogen-alone arm, deep venous thrombosis

choices.label: C
choices.text: Combined arm, hip fracture; estrogen-alone arm, colorectal cancer

choices.label: D
choices.text: Combined arm, invasive breast cancer; estrogen-alone arm, stroke

choices.label: E
choices.text: Combined arm, stroke; estrogen-alone arm, invasive breast cancer

explanation.summary: The combined estrogen-progestogen arm was stopped in 2002 for increased invasive breast cancer; the estrogen-only arm was stopped in 2004 for increased stroke.
explanation.whyCorrect: The trial enrolled 27,347 postmenopausal females aged 50-79 and ran from 1993 to 2004. The conjugated equine estrogens plus medroxyprogesterone acetate arm was discontinued in 2002 because of increased invasive breast cancer, and the estrogen-only arm was discontinued in 2004 because of increased stroke, findings that have shaped prescribing for more than 20 years.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Neither arm was stopped for thromboembolism or endometrial cancer, and unopposed estrogen was given only to females without a uterus.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Endometrial cancer did not end the combined arm; the added progestogen exists specifically to prevent endometrial hyperplasia and cancer.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Fracture reduction and decreased colorectal cancer risk are benefits of hormone therapy, not reasons a trial arm was halted.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The findings are swapped: breast cancer ended the combined arm and stroke ended the estrogen-only arm.

questions.stem: A 68-year-old female whose final menstrual period occurred at age 50 asks to begin systemic hormone therapy for mild hot flashes that have persisted. She has no contraindications. Which of the following best describes her candidacy for treatment?

choices.label: A
choices.text: She falls outside the window of opportunity for initiating systemic therapy

choices.label: B
choices.text: She may use estrogen alone because she is more than 10 years postmenopausal

choices.label: C
choices.text: She requires a progestogen alone because estrogen is unsafe after age 60

choices.label: D
choices.text: She should start combined therapy indefinitely to protect her bone density

choices.label: E
choices.text: She should start high-dose oral estrogen to offset years of deficiency

explanation.summary: Hormone therapy should be started within the window of opportunity, within 10 years of menopause or before age 60, at the lowest effective dose for the shortest duration needed.
explanation.whyCorrect: After the Women's Health Initiative, recommendations call for the lowest effective dose for the shortest duration, initiated within the window of opportunity, meaning within 10 years of menopause or before age 60. At 68 and 18 years postmenopausal, this patient is outside that window, so non-hormonal options are more appropriate for her mild symptoms.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Time since menopause does not remove the need for endometrial protection; unopposed estrogen is only for females who have had a hysterectomy.
whyWrongByChoice.C: A progestogen alone is not a treatment for vasomotor symptoms; it is given to oppose estrogen's endometrial effects.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Indefinite therapy conflicts with the shortest duration needed, and starting late is precisely what the window guidance discourages.
whyWrongByChoice.E: High-dose therapy contradicts the lowest effective dose principle and would amplify thromboembolic and stroke risk.

questions.stem: A 51-year-old female with an intact uterus takes transdermal estradiol with a synthetic progestin. She reports bothersome side effects on the progestin, and repeat testing shows a worsened lipid profile. Which of the following changes to her regimen is most appropriate?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Increase the dose of the synthetic progestin

choices.label: B
choices.text: Replace the progestogen with oral ospemifene

choices.label: C
choices.text: Replace the progestogen with vaginal estrogen cream

choices.label: D
choices.text: Stop the progestogen and continue estradiol alone

choices.label: E
choices.text: Switch the progestin to micronized progesterone

explanation.summary: Micronized progesterone has a more favorable lipid effect and fewer side effects than synthetic progestins while still protecting the endometrium.
explanation.whyCorrect: Progesterone can be delivered orally, transdermally, or via intrauterine systems, and micronized progesterone has a more favorable effect on lipids and fewer side effects than synthetic progestins. Switching preserves the endometrial protection she still needs while addressing both problems.

whyWrongByChoice.A: A higher dose of the same agent would worsen the side effects and lipid changes that prompted the change.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Ospemifene is a SERM approved for dyspareunia from vulvovaginal atrophy and does not provide endometrial protection.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Vaginal estrogen treats local atrophic symptoms; adding more estrogen does not oppose systemic estrogen at the endometrium.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Because she has an intact uterus, unopposed systemic estrogen risks endometrial hyperplasia and cancer.

questions.stem: A 50-year-old female with an intact uterus uses transdermal estradiol for hot flashes but cannot tolerate oral progesterone because of daytime sedation. She still requires endometrial protection. Which of the following is the most appropriate alternative?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Higher-dose transdermal estradiol patch

choices.label: B
choices.text: Intramuscular testosterone every 2 weeks

choices.label: C
choices.text: Levonorgestrel-releasing intrauterine system

choices.label: D
choices.text: Oral ospemifene once daily

choices.label: E
choices.text: Vaginal estrogen tablet twice weekly

explanation.summary: Progesterone can be delivered orally, transdermally, or by intrauterine system, so intolerance of the oral route does not preclude endometrial protection.
explanation.whyCorrect: Females with an intact uterus on systemic estrogen require a progestogen to prevent endometrial hyperplasia and cancer.
